items.body: Across eight untitled pieces, fold/interval develops a musical language in which guitar dyads, granular electronics, filtered resonances and microscopic digital artefacts coexist within carefully articulated sonic environments. By directing attention towards the behaviour of sound itself, its texture, spectral balance and the constantly shifting relationships between one resonance and the next, Giuseppe Ielasi and Fabio Perletta engage in an open exchange that is equally balanced and coherent. The title of the project itself offers an illuminating point of entry. In audio synthesis, wavefolding is a process in which a signal exceeding a certain threshold is folded back onto itself, generating new harmonics and increasingly complex timbral structures instead of simply clipping or distorting. The second half of the title is equally revealing. Throughout the album, Giuseppe Ielasi’s guitar is reduced to two-note dyads—musical intervals—whose quiet interjections provide the elementary material from which Fabio Perletta’s electronic processes unfold. Fold describes a continuous process of sonic transformation; interval refers both to the guitar’s harmonic vocabulary and to the spaces separating successive sonic events. The music continually inhabits both meanings. The dialogue between Ielasi and Perletta never feels predetermined. Repeated figures evolve through minute changes in density, frequency and perspective, while silence functions as an active compositional force, shaping every gesture with remarkable precision. Listening gradually shifts away from isolated sonic events towards intervals in both senses of the word: the relationships between pitches and the spaces separating sounds. Tiny overtone fluctuations, delicate feedback and almost imperceptible transients continually redefine the surrounding acoustic field. Giulia Bruno‘s photographic contribution is integral to the project. Her images of landscapes, architectural structures and technological infrastructures mirror the music’s fascination with hidden systems, suspended attention and processes unfolding beneath the threshold of immediate perception. Sound and image share the same temporal logic, encouraging prolonged observation rather than instant recognition. Ultimately, fold/interval is a record about relationships: between acoustic and electronic sound, presence and absence, transformation and stasis. Every gesture appears with an acute sense of proportion. Like the wavefolding process evoked in its title, it reveals how complexity can emerge from the continuous reshaping of the simplest materials. giulia bruno (self portrait giulia bruno) To find out more we have spoken directly with Ielasi, Perletta and Bruno. Untitled (1–8) feels poised between presence and absence: Giuseppe’s sparse guitar gestures seem to emerge from and dissolve back into Fabio’s electronic textures, while Giulia’s photographs introduce a parallel visual rhythm. How did the three of you develop a shared language across sound and image, and at what point did the project become more than a musical collaboration and evolve into fold/interval itself? Giulia Bruno: fold/interval was born from the desire to create together within a free and anti-hierarchical relational context, where sounds and images can also follow a shared path, without subordination. Our relationship began with mutual respect and with a friendship that developed over time. Recognizing ourselves in what each of us does — and perhaps also in who each of us is through our work — created a solid foundation from which the desire emerged to explore something unexpected together, grounded in a shared trust in looking and listening. The project therefore arises from the desire to bring together thoughts, sensibilities, and intuitions that find their form through shared sounds, images, and silences. Fabio Perletta: fold/interval was never just a musical project; rather, it started as a trio. Before that, Giuseppe and I had been discussing the possibility of collaborating in a broader sense. Giulia and Giuseppe already knew each other well, having collaborated for a long time, so everything naturally found its way into fold/interval, which was conceived as a space for exchange involving different practices and sensibilities, where sound and image could develop together. We aim to find a shared space where listening and looking can influence each other, and where unexpected connections could emerge. The music and the photographs are not separate layers, but different manifestations of a shared process and vision. Giuseppe Ielasi: I have been working with Giulia, on different projects, for more than 15 years. This was mainly on film or installation works. More recently we started discussing about possible live performances, and our first one as a duo happened in June 2025 at the Triennale in Milano. We loved it, but at the same time felt the need to work on something less structured, more open to improvisation and surprises. I also know Fabio since a long time: we shared a few concerts and he published some of my music on 901editions, but most of all we exchanged thoughts, music and spent a lot of time together in the last years. We were ready for a collaboration and started playing and recording together. It was very natural, then, to merge those projects, introducing Giulia to Fabio. My impression is that the shared language was already there, it was just a matter of making things happen. fabio perletta (photo oyamada kuniya) The release includes photographs ranging from natural and architectural environments to technological infrastructures, including an image of the cooling systems of the Barcelona Supercomputing Center. Given the increasing debate around the environmental cost of AI and large-scale computation, were these infrastructures approached primarily as visual forms, or do they also function as reflections on the invisible systems that increasingly shape contemporary life and knowledge production? GB: My work never approaches images solely as visual forms. Rather, the image is a pretext for activation: a way of bringing to light contemporary questions concerning collective issues, research processes, and systems of relation. In this sense, I am interested in deconstructing the aesthetics of the image, removing it from spectacle so that it can become an activator. An activator of processes of change and reflection on how we observe, recognize, and respond to different forms of violence and contradiction. I believe we are often suspended within a constant tension: between hypnosis and impotence, between beauty and fear, between systems of seduction and power and critical awareness. This is why I am interested in working with the landscape — whether natural, technological, architectural, infrastructural, human, or relational — as a space to be read, questioned, and traversed. The infrastructures, and what is reactivated through photography, are therefore not merely formal presences, but signals of broader, often invisible systems that condition the way we live, know, and imagine the future, within an obsessive system of continuous archiving. To look also means asking ourselves what choices we can make in order to build a collectivity capable of coexisting, resisting, and generating new forms of relation. FP: I believe this connection is at the core of fold/interval. The project does not come from a desire to blindly produce new images and sounds, but rather to create a space where attention can be reactivated and where different, heightened forms of perception coexist. We are not interested in spectacularization, our focus is on cultivating attention. The way we work together is based on a process of listening and waiting, allowing each element to emerge without forcing relationships or creating predetermined correspondences. We were drawn to what happens in the space between things: between the visible and the hidden, between what is heard and what is left in silence. In this sense, fold/interval reflects a resistance to the acceleration and saturation that define contemporary production and consumption. This first work seeks to open up a different temporal dimension—one where the viewer and listener are invited to sit with uncertainty, observe the details, and forge their own connections. giuseppe ielasi (photo philip ielasi) The music is remarkably restrained. Guitar notes and chords seem to drift through digital circuitry, leaving large amounts of space between events. Was reduction a conscious compositional strategy from the outset, or did the pieces gradually arrive at this sparse form through a process of subtraction and editing? FP: From my perspective, it is a combination of both. The way Giuseppe and I approach sound within this project stems from a shared interest in creating an environment where every element holds its own weight and presence, allowing unexpected encounters to unfold. Reduction wasn’t a conscious aesthetic choice; it emerged from a desire to let the space breathe and become an active component of the composition. Silence, resonance, and the intervals between events are not mere voids, but structural pillars that give sounds the room to reveal their intrinsic qualities. At the same time, this sparseness was already baked into the sounds we each brought to the table. Giuseppe’s guitar—with its precision and abstract quality—and my stylized electronic textures, which are often pushed toward the extreme areas of the spectrum, come from very different yet complimentary worlds. Throughout the process, we constantly sought an organic balance between these two worlds, letting the clarity and subtle details of the guitar interact with the ambiguity and roughness of the electronics. GI: It’s strange, the music doesn’t feel that restrained to me. There’s constant activity in it, lots of repetitions (but no loops) and the pacing and placing are very deliberate, but somehow the flow feels very natural (the idea of ‘restrain’ somehow suggest that it was ‘forced’, and that is not the case). There was little subtraction, and almost no editing. We suggested basic materials and layers and realized that many of those could co-exist and interacts very naturally. It was a very intuitive, non-formalised process. Giulia, many of your recent texts engage with questions of technological mediation, the overproduction of images, and the difficulty of maintaining spaces of reflection within contemporary systems of visibility. Do you see a connection between those concerns and the aesthetic choices behind Untitled (1–8), which often feels like it is resisting speed, saturation and information overload in favour of slowness, ambiguity and attention? GB: We are connected by a shared way of thinking: the desire not to follow the logics of production, seduction, and spectacularization, but rather the rhythm of our own thought and listening. It is a natural gaze, made of layers but not oversaturation, of words expressed with care, and of a constant search for coherence. There are no predetermined rules or rigid orders of thought, but rather a natural transformation that emerges from the attempt to remove the work from what is immediately displayed. We are interested in what remains suspended, what requires time, what does not immediately offer itself only as an image or as information. The reflection on the macrosystems in which we move as individuals runs through our thinking and our gaze, and also shapes the way we relate to others. Untitled (1–8) emerges from this attention: from the desire to create a space in which sound, image, and word can slow down perception and open up the possibility of a shared rereading of the processes that involve us. FP: I am drawn to the word Giulia mentioned: rhythm. Our biological rhythm—the intrinsic time we need to process our surroundings—differs for everyone, but it is undeniably a means of survival in this violent, vulgar world. To honor it requires welcoming the complex, the unexpected, the unheard, and the unseen. We aim to stay close to this idea, not in a literal, romantic, or strictly political sense, but as a practice that resists the pressure to produce immediate meaning or visibility. Giulia’s reflection on overproduction and the saturation of images deeply informs how we approach both sound and vision: not as materials to be quickly consumed, but as processes demanding time. The project seeks to create a space where perception can remain open and non-finalised, where things are not immediately resolved into information or representation. Instead, it sustains an alternative internal tempo—one that allows for hesitation, repetition, and return. fold/interval is described not only as an audiovisual project but also as a publishing platform. Beyond this first release, how do you envision the project developing? Are future editions likely to continue exploring the relationship between image, sound and material publication, or do you see fold/interval evolving into a broader framework for collaborations, research projects and new commissions? GB: Starting from the coming together of our conversations, we did not want to place any limit on the project’s transformation. We believe in a path made of coherence, but also of responses to research processes that can change, expand, and take on new forms over time, just as we ourselves change over time. For us, collaboration means first and foremost engaging in dialogue and confrontation. We have not placed any limit on this exchange, except for the desire to do it with people who share with us a vision of the world in which aesthetics is never placed above relationships, research, and the search for meaning in life. In this sense, fold/interval may continue to explore the relationship between image, sound, and material publication, but it may also open itself to other forms: collaborations, research, commissions, dialogues, and processes that have not yet been anticipated. What interests us is that it remains a living space, capable of transforming without losing coherence. FP: For me, fold/interval is less of a fixed container and more of an open ecology, inherently built to evolve. The idea of the publishing platform naturally stems from a desire to give a physical, tangible form to time and thought, which is why the material aspect will always remain a core interest. Looking ahead, I imagine fold/interval evolving as a flexible framework that could manifest as a physical edition, a sound installation, a research residency, or simply a space for shared dialogue. Future editions might not always look or sound the same, it will simply follow the needs of the encounters and questions that emerge along the way. GI: What interests me is to collaborate on a project that’s very open, hard to define and might even be confusing at times. We released an edition with a cd and a set of photos, a short film on our website and we’re co-curating some events and sound installations at “settantaventidue” in Milano. But we also exist as a label / publishing platform (more editions, with or without music, might appear soon and those could include other collaborators) and we’re planning some concerts, residencies and installations for the next months. So, yes, it’s definitely evolving and I’m very curious to see what will happen. (Gianmarco Del Re)

Moving through modernized, mechanized electronic flutter Such sleek, rhythmic glitch sees rinse.repeat at it again with this oversized extended player, running just over twenty-four minutes and moving through modernized, mechanized electronic flutter, opening with “ERR_LOOP: Pleasant Failure.” After all this time, its “errors,” under an imprint committed to keeping them “clean,” continue to cultivate minute sonic acrobatics from start to finish. With its second volume leaning into what could be further musical constructs, “SWEET_CORRUPT” glides along through minimal technoid shifts, while the Arovane-leaning “The Last Pattern We Shared” and “AXM_02::LOOP_DESYNC” work through a relaxed infusion of bleep-breaks. The back-half triplet of Brain Axiom Vol.2 dissolves into an accumulation of everything that has come before: “A Feeling With No Output” brings tonal color, “BRAINMAP_FRAGMENT_v3” flickers through beat-driven landscapes, and closer “CRPT_SEQ:AXM” pushes it all toward a sweetly melancholic (and slightly disjointed) intersection, bringing everything together with focused restraint. system.log>>> [Recovered audio signature matches AXIOM-Vol.2-grade entropy]>>> [Loop recursion depth: INCREASING]>>> [System awareness protocol: ACTIVATED]>>> [Pattern self-recognition: CONFIRMED]ERROR SIGNATURE: [///loop:remember:feel:break]░▒▓██▒▒░┈┈┈┈──> Brain Axiom Vol.2 complete. <──┈┈┈▒██▓▒░░⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿the machine now knows it is broken.and that knowledge is the only beautiful thing left.⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿⣿  Brain Axiom Vol.2 is available on Clean Error. items.body: Review by BrufordFreak — WARNING: This is a release of material recorded in 1972 that represents two different bands containing some of the same musicians that just happen to overlap in that year.Recorded 1972, unreleased until 1999. I was turned on to Riff Raff a few weeks ago so I've been slowly getting to know their music and their story. I was immediately impressed (and astounded that I'd never heard of them--even in my 18 years associated with ProgArchives) by all of their albums--which made the decision of which album to review first very difficult since, in learning their story I'd discovered that their first records--their debut album--had never been released at the time of its creation. But I do like to get to know a band/artist in chronological order if I can, so, of course I want to start with their first album: the problem is that their first album that became known to the public was their second album, the eponymously titled Riff Raff from 1973; Outside Looking In never reached public ears until 1999! As I've been listening to this album I've come to know that the opening 39 minutes represent material performed by the band's original lineup, a project calling themselves, STRABISMUS, which recorded this material in London in 1972. The second 23-minutes of "Bonus Tracks" represents Roger Sutton and Tommy Eyre's more-Jazz-oriented band, RIFF RAFF. Sutton, himself a former member of Brian Auger's Trinity project, continued to develop Riff Raff for the next few years with keyboardist Tommy Eyre, guitarist Peter Kirtley, and drummer Aureo De Souza before giving himself completely to Ian Carr's NUCLEUS. Peter Kirtley's most notable credit post-Riff Raff was his contribution to an album that has always remained dear to me: Yes' Alan White's first solo album, 1976's Ramshackled., while also joining The Pentangle during their tenure in the 1990s. Tommy Eyre himself was a product of previous collaborations with Aynsley Dunbar and Mark-Almond. He would go on to make significant contributions to successful albums by Zzebra, Alex Harvey, Gerry Rafferty, Gary Moore, John Martyn, Greg Lake, Michael Schenker, and Wham!. Singer Alan Marshall was hired by Zzebra (at the suggestion of the band's newcomer keyboard player, Tommy Eyre) as their singer for the 1974-75 sessions and tour that would produce the material for the band's classic sophomore album, Panic, as well as a third and fourth album--which weren't released until 1999 and 2001, respectively. Brasilian-born percussionist/drummer Aureo De Souza would also find himself hired by Ian Carr, as a percussionist, for Nucleus' mid-70s classic funk albums, but the material he recorded with the band never reached the public as part of their studio album releases--only surfaced years later (mostly in the 21st Century) when record labels Vertigo, Andy Gray's BGO (Beat Goes On) Records, and Esoteric Recordings began releasing retrospective CDs that included outtakes and live performances.Line-up / Musicians:As STRABISMUS:- Alan Marshall / vocals- Martin Ball / guitar- Tommy Eyre / Hammond organ, keyboards, acoustic guitar- Richie Dalton / saxophone- Roger Sutton (Brian Auger's Trinity) / bass, acoustic guitars, vocals- Rob Coombes (Juicy Lucy, Stealers Wheel) / drums, percussion & acoustic guitar- Joe Peters (Jackie Jocko) / drumsAs RIFF RAFF:- Alan Marshall / vocals- Peter Kirtley / guitar- Kenny Slade (Joe Cocker) / drums- Aureo De Souza / drums, percussion- Tommy Eyre / Hammond organ, keyboards, acoustic guitar- Richie Dalton / saxophone- Roger Sutton / bass, acoustic guitars, vocals(As Strabismus):1. "Outside Looking In" (9:12) opening a debut album with a long-playing jam is bold and brave! I guess it lets the listener know what kind of band they thought of themselves (unless the song order was altered over time or never decided at the time of its first creation): not hit makers. The material here is heavy, fully Rock 'n' Roll with some creative touches, nice construction and delivery, more akin to hard rockin' guitar-jammin' bands like Cream, Spirit, Mountain, Humble Pie, etc. (18.125/20)2. "The Blind Man" (8:16) opens with a much more acoustic orientation: bluesy piano, percussion and drums, Hammond organ, acoustic guitars, and vocals from a gravelly-voiced male singer. I'm immediately reminded of Southern Rock bands like The Allman Brothers and The Marshall Tucker Band. The cessation of the vocal leads into a rockin' jam with saxophonist Richie Dalton really letting loose with some wild screaming sounds. But then there is this totally unexpected transition around the five-minute mark into a more delicate, almost folk-Mexican acoustic guitar motif in which I believe four of the band members drop their instruments to pick up acoustic guitars and then what sounds like professional choral singers join in singing "Close your eyes, I can feel you" over and over before Alan rejoins to sing over them to the song's close. Very cool and unexpected song and music. (18.25/20)3. "Bach B. Minor Prelude" (2:58) a full solo on a church organ! Luscious! Another very cool and unexpected song. (9/10)4. "Feeling Paranoic" (0:43) a theatric song that feels like an outtake from Judas' or Jesus' performances in Jesus Christ Superstar. (4.375/5)5. "Buthelezi" (3:42) drummer Joe Peters leads the way through a drum & percussion jam that involves Rob Coombes and others. I love this kind of stuff--especially in live performances (or to participate in) but I'm not sure of its place on a studio album: it seems as if this space could/should have been given to a proper full-band song composition. But then I'm beginning to wonder if there is a conceptual theme, intention, or organization to the album. Anyone? (9/10)6. "So You Want To Be Free" (10:52) the music here is a return to the raw hard rock that we encountered with the album's opening song, "Outside Looking In." The raw, gravelly voice of Alan Marshall is back up front for the first couple minutes, then the music transitions into a vamp governed by a quick three-note riff that is repeated over and over while everyone just jams over and around it: saxophone, electric piano, drums, even, eventually, electric guitar. The sax solo is the best of the three; guitarist Martin Ball is not "fully formed" yet though he does sound better once the vamp slows down and punctuates itself like some Swamp Blues and he starts shredding for speed. (I guess he needed to get warmed up.) Martin's solo section ends with some well-timed whole-band chord bashing which sounds really cool and inventive--like something King Crimsonian--but then the music turns to smoother blues rock over which two male vocalists sing, gentler, harmonizing, before the music begins to slowly devolve into just a few percussion/cymbal noises and guitar and electric piano notes. Brilliant--and so creative! (18.25/20)7. "Changes" (3:23) acoustic guitar accompanying Alan's singing on what sounds like a cover but apparently is just another of the album's Sutton/Coombes compositions. Simple and nice; definitely could have been developed into something bigger. (8.667/10)Total time: 39:06A-/4.5 stars; a near-masterpiece of eclectic Southern Power Rock.Bonus Tracks (as Riff Raff):8. "Child Of The Summer" (5:59) a jazzy feeling song with a syncopated, complex construction and feeling vocal performance (reminiscent of Allan's performance on Allan White's Ramshakled). After the chorus the band revs up and becomes more rock-forceful--but it's still good! Nice wah-wah-ed electric guitar work, great background vocal work, great dirty electric piano, and awesome bass, drums, and percussion at the base. This is the rock-perspective to Jazz-Rock Fusion that I've been hoping to find more of! (9.25/10)9. "For Every Dog" (4:05) a truly awesome acoustic Southern Rock song that should/could've been a radio-friendly hit back in 1973. Great weave of instrumental performances blessed with a weave of awesome group harmonized vocals. Shades of The Youngbloods, Crosby, Stills, Nash & Young, Ozark Mountain Daredevils, Pure Prairie League, or the early Doobie Brothers or Eagles. (9.5/10)10. "Morning" (5:57) piano-based soft bluesy light folk/Americana pop arranged with an odd triple-hop at the end of each measure. The singer is mostly backed by another harmonizing vocalist (or vocal track) while acoustic guitars, bass, and gentle drums back/accompany the piano and singers. I believe a flute may also be in the mix though its replication of the piano's legato may be just be a second piano track. A very pleasant, not-quite-Cat Stevens, not-quite-Harry Nilsson tune. (8.875/10) 11. "The Garden" (6:59) bluesy solo piano opens this for about 30 seconds before Allan and the background choir vocalists join in. The song sounds almost like a church/liturgical piece--something one might hear in the countryside villages of Ireland. Strummed 12-string acoustic guitar, bass, congas, and drums slowly, almost surreptitiously, join in as Allan gives his hear and soul to his vocal performance. There is definitely a flute in this one--entering just before the piano ramps things up with more volume. There is a little Dave Mason "We Just Disagree" sound and feel here. Then Allan really brings it: belting out with two minutes to go but then things quickly de-escalate as he and his backing singers sing softly about the importance of our ancestor/elders. It drags on a bit but it's a very nice song with a great vocal performance and some nice, positive lyrics. (13.375/15)Total time: 24:00A-/five stars; a minor masterpiece of Jazz- and Rock-informed Southern Folk Rock.Total Time: 62:06 I don't usually review "bonus" material in my album reviews (because I want to treat the material as it would have been heard in the year it was recorded) but then when this was (finally) released in 1999 it arrived in CD format and, thus, being its first exposure to the public, should be heard as a whole. The problem, of course, comes with the fact that the material is really the result of two completely different bands: one that never really persisted, the other which came out and toured for a year or so before scattering its members across the musical spectrum in the UK and US. I definitely like both "albums" though the Riff Raff "bonus" material is more of the kind of stuff that I'd listen to over and over. (I almost want to rate the two "albums" separately! A-/five stars; a minor masterpiece of Jazz-infused Southern Folk Rock.

items.body: Atrición is the sort of record that seems to have been built under fluorescent light, with the smell of disinfectant somewhere nearby and history banging its head against the walls. Santiago Nicolás wrote much of it in an oncology center, and that circumstance hangs over the album with a terrible physical clarity. The body here is material: cells change, systems fail, pressure accumulates, and time works patiently on everything it touches. Nicolás places that fact beside political violence, invasion, borders, archives, and inherited trauma, finding a shared logic in processes that advance by occupation and erosion rather than spectacle. That could have produced a record swollen with significance. Instead, Atrición stays severe, compact, and rhythmically exact. Its drums hit with the blunt economy of DAF and Nitzer Ebb, while the synths carry the cold forward motion of contemporary techno. Suicide lurks in the repetition, Cabaret Voltaire in the sense that machinery can become a social instrument, and Schwefelgelb in the clipped, bodily momentum. Nicolás keeps tightening the screws until repetition stops feeling like recurrence and starts behaving like pressure. This is where the album becomes genuinely nasty in the best sense. A beat returns, a distorted percussion figure acquires another layer, a synthesizer line keeps digging into the same patch of ground, and suddenly you understand accumulation as an experience rather than a concept. Violence, in this framework, survives through systems, habits, documents, buildings, borders, and bodies that continue carrying its consequences after the visible event has passed. Atrición makes persistence feel physical. The lyrics work through archives, silence, trauma, and accountability without collapsing into slogans. Nicolás favours metaphor, which gives the songs room to operate somewhere between private memory and public history. He is interested in transmission: what passes from one generation to another, what institutions preserve by omission, what a body remembers despite every attempt at erasure. The music answers with repetition so stubborn that it begins to resemble bureaucracy with a kick drum. By the end, Atrición feels like a controlled study in pressure: biological, political, historical, rhythmic. Catastrophe often advances by degrees, through small permissions and repeated injuries. He builds music for that recognition, and the result is frightening precisely because it moves with such discipline, until pressure itself becomes its own evidence. Listen to Atrición below and order the EP here. Atrición by Santiago Nicolás Nicolás has spent more than a decade moving through electronic music, noise, experimental composition, and post-punk, including work with The Deadly Affair, Access Device, Ángel de la Guarda, and Föllakzoid’s live lineup. Atrición compresses that experience into a language of hard surfaces and accumulating force. The production is clean enough to expose every impact, yet abrasive enough to keep the record from becoming sterile. Follow Santiago Nicolás: Bandcamp Instagram The post Chilean Techno-Industrial Producer Santiago Nicolás Performs an Autopsy on Trauma in “Atrición” EP appeared first on Post-Punk.com.

items.body: Depeche Mode, the English electronic band from Basildon, Essex, released “Construction Time Again” on 22 August 1983 through Mute Records. The album turns 43 this year. It was the band’s third studio album and reached number 6 on the UK Albums Chart. Daniel Miller produced the album together with Depeche Mode, with Gareth Jones engineering. Recording took place at the Garden studio in London, mixing at Hansa Mischraum in Berlin, and mastering at CBS Studios in London. The band built much of the album around sampled found sounds, recorded on a Synclavier and an Emulator, including metal being struck and other industrial noises. “Construction Time Again” was the first Depeche Mode studio album to feature Alan Wilder as a full member; he co-wrote two of the album’s songs. The nine-track album runs “Love, in Itself,” “More Than a Party,” “Pipeline,” “Everything Counts,” “Two Minute Warning,” “Shame,” “The Landscape Is Changing,” “Told You So” and “And Then…” Mute released “Everything Counts” as the lead single on 11 July 1983, ahead of the album; it reached number 6 on the UK Singles Chart. “Love, in Itself” followed as the second single on 19 September 1983 and peaked at number 21. “Construction Time Again” followed “A Broken Frame” (1982) and preceded “Some Great Reward” (1984), the album that produced “People Are People.” About Depeche Mode Vince Clarke, Martin Gore, Dave Gahan and Andy Fletcher formed Depeche Mode in Basildon, Essex, in 1980, taking their name from a French fashion magazine. The band signed to Daniel Miller’s independent label Mute Records and released the synth-pop debut album “Speak & Spell” in 1981. Clarke left the band after that album to form Yazoo with Alison Moyet, and Gore took over as the band’s main songwriter. Depeche Mode continued as a trio for “A Broken Frame” (1982), then expanded to a four-piece with the addition of Alan Wilder for “Construction Time Again” (1983), the album that introduced sampled industrial sounds and engineer Gareth Jones to the band’s productions. The Miller and Jones production team continued with Depeche Mode through “Some Great Reward” (1984), “Black Celebration” (1986), “Music for the Masses” (1987) and “Violator” (1990), the album that produced “Personal Jesus” and “Enjoy the Silence.” Wilder left the band in 1995 after “Songs of Faith and Devotion” (1993); Depeche Mode continued as a trio of Gahan, Gore and Fletcher, releasing “Ultra” (1997), “Exciter” (2001), “Playing the Angel” (2005), “Sounds of the Universe” (2009), “Delta Machine” (2013) and “Spirit” (2017). Fletcher died in May 2022, and Gahan and Gore released “Memento Mori” as a duo in 2023, touring behind a Mexico City concert film titled “M.” “Construction Time Again,” released 22 August 1983, marked the start of the band’s move from straightforward synth-pop toward the denser, sample-driven productions that shaped its subsequent albums.

items.body: Canadian netlabel Panospria released “I-II-III”, the debut album under the Silver Shadow name, on 15 July 2026. It runs to 26 tracks across three volumes gathered into a single digital set, sold in MP3 and FLAC from 15 Canadian dollars, and it moves between IDM, ambient, drone and minimal techno. The release page presents the album as three distinct volumes compiled into one, and as the latest work of a long-standing name on the label. It never prints that name: “Having recently relocated to France from Canada, keen listeners will surely deduce the identity of this mainstay on our label. New country, new alias, new directions in music.” The label’s own announcement is less coy than the release page. It presents Silver Shadow as the new alias of the artist formerly recording as Silent Q and Gyges. Both of those names belong to Paul Keeley, a Montreal electronic producer whose Gyges album “Composite Massive” was Panospria’s second release in 2004 and who has issued deep and progressive house under his own name through Thinner, Epsilonlab and Anjunadeep. The Silver Shadow Bandcamp page gives the artist’s location as Paris. What is on the Silver Shadow album ‘I-II-III’ The three volumes are not new to the same degree. Volume I is the eight-track album “I”, put on Bandcamp on 26 July 2022, and volume II is the ten-track “II” from 22 November 2024; the remaining eight tracks, from “Delores” to “Matte”, appear here for the first time. II by Silver Shadow Track titles run as compressed fragments throughout: “Aieesqvb96”, “nFU-VHToT”, “HshShsHs”, “HpnoTod”, “Grgwld”, “Dickenszs”. In order the album reads Aieesqvb96, Fulter, Plyurs, nFU-VHToT, Crunge, Duke, Spong, Purf, Ghosnen, AmbWks, Mmoonn, TheLab, Pull, HshShsHs, HpnoTod, Unstld, Grgwld, Roogah, Delores, KiBC8, NewWav, Sheets, Dickenszs, Krud, Thumb and Matte. About Silver Shadow and Panospria Silver Shadow first appeared on Bandcamp on 3 April 2020 with the five-track “A”, followed by “I” in 2022 and “II” in 2024, so the Panospria set is a label debut rather than a first release under the alias. Panospria itself grew out of the Canadian prairies around the turn of the millennium and put out its first offering, the “Alphaform” compilation, in 2002 with Dublin’s Psychonavigation. The label was properly established in Montreal that same year and was among the earliest to treat the MP3 as a release format in its own right. It moved with its operators, running from Montreal until 2008, then Vancouver, then Saskatoon from 2022. Alongside the catalogue it ran two concert series: Textures in Montreal and Quiet City in Vancouver, the latter reaching 70 editions over a decade. In 2007 the Panospria catalogue was folded into the Montreal netlabel No Type, which has been active since 1998 and also runs Annexe, BricoLodge, Nishi and Sine Fiction; Panospria has operated as a No Type sublabel since. Paul Keeley’s connection to the label goes back almost to the start. The Gyges record “Composite Massive” carried the second catalogue number in 2004, and he has since appeared on Panospria releases by Heart & Soul, Shoebomber, Arnau Sala and N4K3D D1G1TS. “I-II-III” is the first Silver Shadow release Panospria has issued, and by the label’s account the first since the move from Canada to France.

items.body: German EBM and electro label emmobiz records releases “V.A. 19. Elektrisch Festival” on 24 October 2026, the same day as the 19th Elektrisch Festival at Club Seilerstraße in Zwickau. The 10-inch is pressed on brown vinyl, limited to 222 copies, and sells for 16.99 euro through the label’s own shop. Six tracks from five acts fill the two sides. The record continues an annual series that the label has run since the festival returned in 2024, following the red-vinyl 16th edition and the 17th edition 10-inch, and the 18th, which split across an EBM Edition and a Synth Pop Edition earlier this year. emmobiz describes the Elektrisch series as the only festival compilation of its kind carrying rare or exclusive tracks from the acts on the bill. What is on the 19. Elektrisch Festival 10-inch Four of the five acts on the record play the festival. Portion Control, this year’s headliner, does not appear on the compilation. The label fills the gap with two bonus tracks by acts outside the bill. A1: Escalator, “Utolsókor (Short)”, 3:47 A2: Oszylayter, “we’re the noise”, 4:01 A3: Cyborg Projekt X, “Native Terror” (Vinyl Edit), 3:49 B1: Krieg-B, “kill the light” (V111 Mix), 5:20 B2: Sabotage Q.C.Q.C., “Heidenangst” (Drumatic), 6:05 B3: TöT, “Diers Irae” (Rough Mix), 2:27 The two bonus cuts on the B-side reach outside the festival line-up. Sabotage Q.C.Q.C. are a German electro act who released through Spin Records and EMI Electrola in the 1990s; “Heidenangst” first appeared on their 1996 album “Sexploitation Cinema” and returned in remixed form on the 1997 maxi-single “Schlager”. The version here is a new remake made for this record. Closing the compilation, the Marseille electro-punk and EBM band TöT contribute “Diers Irae”. Escalator, the Budapest EBM band founded in 1988 by 2RT+TB, took their starting point from Kraftwerk and have released since 1989. Oszylayter bring electropunk and breakbeat from Germany. Krieg-B, the Franco-Belgian project Dominique Lallement and Benoît Buyse started in June 2023, follow their emmobiz debut “War Drums’ Resonance” with the album “Concrete Dominion”, which the label also dates to 24 October. About the Elektrisch Festival and emmobiz records The Elektrisch Festival ran five editions in Zwickau between 2007 and 2010, from the 11th to the 15th, at the city’s BPM Club. It then stopped for 14 years. emmobiz records brought it back in 2024 with the 16th edition at Club Seilerstraße, which sold out in advance behind Calva Y Nada, Cat Rapes Dog, Digital Factor and Accessory. The 17th followed in October 2025 and the 18th ran over two evenings in February 2026. The 19th takes place on 24 October 2026 with Portion Control, Escalator, Oszylayter, Cyborg Projekt X and Krieg-B; doors open at 19:00 and the music starts at 20:00. emmobiz records is run by Jörg Freier from Oelsnitz in the Erzgebirge, Saxony, and specialises in industrial, EBM and synthpop. The label stopped operating at the end of 2017 and relaunched on 22 August 2024 with a vinyl reissue of Tyske Ludder’s “Bombt Die Mörder?”. Since then it has reissued the Calva Y Nada catalogue on picture disc, pressed Apoptygma Berzerk’s “Kathy’s Song XXV”, and put out records by Second Decay, Blind Passengers, Fairlight Children and Piston Damp. It organises the festival as well as documenting it, and the 10-inch goes on sale the day the doors open.

items.body: Chicago post-punk and industrial duo Bellhead play 14 United States dates between 28 August and 4 October 2026 on the “If I Can’t Break Your Heart Then No One Will” tour, announced on 21 August. The run opens at the Cactus Club in Milwaukee and crosses the Midwest, Great Plains, Southwest and South before closing at Club Area 51 in Salt Lake City. Tickets are sold by each venue. The tour takes its name from “Threats (If I Can’t Break Your Heart)”, the John Weaver-directed video Bellhead put out in June 2026 and the first clip to show Karen Righeimer and Ivan Russia unmasked. The band have since posted two 2026 laurels for it: Best Low Budget Music Video at the Hollywood Best Indie Film Awards and Best Director Music Video at the Tokyo Film and Screenplay Awards. Two dates carry a festival billing. The Albuquerque show on 4 September is part of New Mexico Goth Fest 2026 and shares a bill with eight other acts, and the Salt Lake City date on 4 October falls under The Dark Arts Festival of Utah 2026. On 19 September in Little Rock the duo appear on a bill with PIG and Cyanotic, a single overlap with PIG’s own Hurt People tour rather than a shared leg. Bellhead tour dates for 2026 28 August – Cactus Club, Milwaukee, WI, with Spectra and Vic Dagger 1 September – Coven, Omaha, NE, with X-ID and Dread Portal 2 September – Kirby’s Beer Store, Wichita, KS, with Seven And A Switchblade and Evening Gown 3 September – Crypt, Denver, CO, with eHpH and Hypersomnia 4 September – Launchpad, Albuquerque, NM, New Mexico Goth Fest 2026, with Thief, Hex Cassette, Future Club, Zero Batz, Somno Profundante, Sndwavs, BB Doom and DJ Ordo Amoris 5 September – Resonant Head, Oklahoma City, OK, with Mechanical Flesh, Blood Bells, Othering and Later Laine 6 September – Kickback Bar, Houston, TX, with Polybius Cabinet and TRB 7 September – The Crypt, New Orleans, LA, with Livernois and Chasm Comfort 17 September – Rose Bowl Tavern, Urbana, IL, at Bat Factory 18 September – Hi Tone, Memphis, TN 19 September – Birdie’s, Little Rock, AR, with PIG and Cyanotic 20 September – Fubar, St. Louis, MO, with Spicy Kitty and Bitchface 2 October – Witches’ Brew O.M.G., Lincoln, NE, with Moon Pigeon, The Trauma Center and Bungee Jumping Jesus 4 October – Club Area 51, Salt Lake City, UT, at The Dark Arts Festival of Utah 2026 What Bellhead are touring behind The current catalogue centres on “Threats”, first issued on 8 April 2025 and reissued in June 2026 as a ten-track expanded edition on yellow vinyl. Side A carries the five original songs, and side B collects remixes by Christopher Hall and Walter Flakus of Stabbing Westward, Clubdrugs, Frontal Boundary and the band themselves. Threats by Bellhead Their most recent standalone release is “The The Empty”, a cover of the Le Tigre song, put on Bandcamp on 14 February 2026 through Oppressive Sky Records. Neil Strauch recorded and mixed it, Carl Saff mastered it, and the artwork is Righeimer’s. About Bellhead Bellhead formed in Chicago in 2019 around a line-up of two basses and a drum machine, with no guitar. Karen Righeimer plays low bass and sings, and Ivan Russia plays high bass, sings and programmes the drums. The duo release through Oppressive Sky Records. The discography opens with the 2019 track “Fire Control”, whose Ordinary Mammal remix Side-Line offered as a free download in the Face The Beat: Session 5 profile series. “Unicorn Bones” followed in 2020 and “Dead Lights” in 2021. The single “Nothing As It Seams” arrived in June 2022, the same summer the pair placed tracks on two compilations and toured heavily. The EP “Good Intentions” came out in May 2023 ahead of a US East Coast run with Clay People, and a Prince cover, “I Would Die 4 U”, sits in the catalogue alongside it. “Threats” was announced in March 2025 and reviewed by Side-Line that June. The expanded vinyl edition and the title-track video were announced in June 2026. On the road the duo have supported Stabbing Westward, Clan of Xymox, PIG, Julien-K, Christian Death and Powerman 5000. On the autumn 2026 run they headline, with local and regional support billed at almost every stop.

items.body: Chicago industrial and darkwave artist I Ya Toyah released “Closer”, a cover of the Nine Inch Nails song, on 21 August 2026 through her own label Femme Fatale Records. It is a digital single, and it arrives with a video the same week. On Bandcamp the artist describes the release in a single line: “This is the cover of Nine Inch Nail’s song.” Closer by I Ya Toyah The original was written by Michael Trent Reznor and appeared on Nine Inch Nails‘ 1994 album “The Downward Spiral”. I Ya Toyah produced this version with Johnny K, who also mixed it. Howie Weinberg mastered the track and Angelica Dulany supplied the artwork. Publishing runs through Leaving Hope Music and TVT Music, with the cover licensed through Easy Song Licensing. “Closer” is the third single I Ya Toyah has issued through Femme Fatale Records this year, after the two-track “Feelings” on 1 May and “Apology” on 26 June. Johnny K mixed and produced all three, and Howie Weinberg mastered them. Her press release describes the run as a completed trilogy about the forces that shape identity. The ‘Closer’ video The video was filmed and directed by Alex Zarek, who edited it with I Ya Toyah. The concept is hers. Angelica Dulany handled production assistance and additional direction, Janet Debris did makeup and Allison Ciletti managed the location. It went up on her own YouTube channel on 21 August 2026. The single is on Bandcamp and on the usual streaming services through a single smart link. About I Ya Toyah I Ya Toyah is the solo project of Ania Tarnowska, a Polish-born musician, producer and engineer based in the Chicago area. The name comes from Polish, where the spoken phrase reads as “it’s just me”. She trained on classical guitar, piano and voice as a child, studied music business and audio engineering at the SAE Institute in 2016, and started the project in 2017 with the single “Funeral For Love”. The debut album “Code Blue” followed on 26 October 2018, self-released, with the single “Farewell – Mirrors Don’t Lie” alongside it. The catalogue after that ran quickly. “Code Blue Reloaded” and “Code Blue Revelations” both landed in 2020, the five-part EP “Out of Order” in 2021 and the acoustic EP “Ghosts” in 2022. “Panic Room” arrived in 2023, produced with Walter Flakus of Stabbing Westward, whose US dates she opened that year. Flakus also worked on the “I am the Fire” EP and the album “DRAMA”, both 2024, the year Side-Line covered her video for ‘Fraud’ and talked to her about the new album. She has been a member of The Joy Thieves since 2019 and toured with Pigface the same year. Remixers and collaborators across the catalogue include Rhys Fulber, who remixed “Flashback” in 2019, Tim Skold, who remixed “Motion” in 2020, and Julian Beeston of Nitzer Ebb, whose “We The People”, “Higher Than The Sun” and “Crazy Horses” all feature her. She has also remixed PIG’s “The New Disorder”. In 2024 she toured the United States with Orgy and Cold and played her first European dates supporting Front Line Assembly, and she returned to Europe in February and March 2026 as direct support on KMFDM’s tour. Femme Fatale Records, her own imprint, has carried her releases since 2024 and now issues “Closer”.

items.body: Rammstein, the German Neue Deutsche Härte band, released their second studio album, “Sehnsucht,” on 22 August 1997 through Motor Music in Europe and Slash Records in the United States. The album turns 29 this year. “Sehnsucht” followed the band’s 1995 debut, “Herzeleid,” and includes the singles “Engel” and “Du hast.” Rammstein recorded “Sehnsucht” between November 1996 and July 1997 at Temple Studios in St. Paul’s Bay, Malta, produced again by Jacob Hellner with the band and mixed by Ronald Prent. The eleven-track album runs “Sehnsucht,” “Engel,” “Tier,” “Bestrafe mich,” “Du hast,” “Bück dich,” “Spiel mit mir,” “Klavier,” “Alter Mann,” “Eifersucht” and “Küss mich (Fellfrosch).” North American and Japanese CD editions added English-language versions of “Engel” and “Du hast” as bonus tracks. “Engel” was released as the lead single on 1 April 1997 and reached gold status in Germany on 23 May 1997; “Du hast” followed as the second single, entering the German singles chart at number five in August 1997. “Sehnsucht” reached number one on the German album chart within two weeks of release and later became the only entirely German-language album certified platinum in the United States by the RIAA. “Sehnsucht” streams on Spotify. About Rammstein Rammstein formed in Berlin in 1994. Guitarist Richard Kruspe, who had left East Germany in 1989, began working with bassist Oliver Riedel and drummer Christoph Schneider in 1993 and recruited Till Lindemann, then a drummer in the band First Arsch, as vocalist. Guitarist Paul Landers and keyboardist Christian “Flake” Lorenz, both formerly of the East German band Feeling B, completed the lineup in 1994. The band took its name from the 1988 Ramstein air show disaster, adding an extra “m.” Motor Music signed Rammstein and released the debut single “Du riechst so gut” in August 1995, followed by the debut album “Herzeleid” that September. Rammstein began recording “Sehnsucht” at Temple Studios in Malta in November 1996 while still touring behind “Herzeleid.” Motor Music released the album on 22 August 1997, and its US release through Slash Records led to a four-year world tour, including a 1998 run on the Family Values Tour alongside Korn, Ice Cube, Orgy and Limp Bizkit, and the live album “Live aus Berlin” (1999). Rammstein signed with Universal Music and released “Mutter” in 2001, “Reise, Reise” in 2004, “Rosenrot” in 2005 and “Liebe ist für alle da” in 2009, followed by a self-titled seventh album in 2019 and “Zeit” in 2022. Motor Music issued a remastered anniversary edition of “Sehnsucht” on 9 June 2023. In 2023, German prosecutors opened an investigation into sexual misconduct allegations against Lindemann and closed it later that year, stating no evidence was found to support criminal charges. Rammstein’s catalog has continued to draw outside attention: Swedish dark synth act Priest released a cover of “Engel” in 2023. Lindemann has continued to record outside the band, releasing the single “Es brennt” in March 2026. The anniversary of “Sehnsucht” places the album back in Rammstein’s timeline as the release that took the band from Germany to a global stage.

items.body: Hocico needs no introduction to any fan of Dark-Electro. The Mexican duo has been active continuously since 1993, delivering countless hits and brilliant albums. This new album took a little longer to arrive—around four years—and is available with an extra disc and/or vinyl featuring six additional tracks, including three remixes, one of them by Funker Vogt. With “Unseen Horror Scenes”, Hocico takes aim at various aspects of our contemporary world. Our environment has been in decline for some time, providing a potent source of inspiration for the duo. Musically, the album contains classic, instantly recognizable Hocico tracks infused with a heavy dose of power and aggression. They remain relentless in this regard, yet highly effective in their compositions and rage-filled vocals. However, the album also seeks to introduce some innovation. We encounter various experiments, ranging from pure Electro-Punk and a breakbeat-driven track to Cinematic instrumentals and even a song featuring a touch of Rap. Notably, the main album contains only one Spanish-language track, which is a departure from their usual approach. Hocico has been trying to introduce some evolution into their work over the years, an effort I certainly applaud. Unfortunately, they do not quite succeed on this record. Despite a few strong tracks, I am left feeling somewhat unsatisfied. “Unseen Horror Scenes” has merit on many levels, but it is certainly not the album I would choose to introduce Hocico to someone who has just discovered the Dark-Electro scene. Not every album can be the best. (Rating:7). Listen to “The Screen”: The Screen by Hocico About Hocico Hocico is the Mexican electro-industrial duo of cousins Erik Garcia (Erk Aicrag, vocals and lyrics) and Oscar Mayorga (Racso Agroyam, synthesizers and programming). The pair formed the project in Mexico City in 1993, taking their stage names as reversals of their given names, and played their first concert on 18 February 1994. Early cassette releases such as “Autoagresión Persistente” and “Misuse, Abuse And Accident” in 1994 and “Triste Desprecio” in 1996 were self-released. The studio albums that followed include “Odio Bajo El Alma” in 1997, “El Día De La Ira” in 1998, “Sangre Hirviente” in 1999, “Signos De Aberracion” in 2002, “Wrack And Ruin” in 2004, “Memorias Atrás” in 2008, “Tiempos De Furia” in 2010, “El Último Minuto (Antes De Que Tu Mundo Caiga)” in 2012, “Ofensor” in 2015, “The Spell Of The Spider” in 2017, “Artificial Extinction” in 2019 and “HyperViolent” in 2022. The duo records for Out Of Line. Recent releases on the label include the four-track “The Screen” EP in March 2025 and the collaboration with Prayers on “Hey Tú” in November 2025, expanded into a four-track EP in December 2025. “Unseen Horror Scenes” arrives four years after “HyperViolent” and was announced by Side-Line in May 2026.

items.body: On “Londi”, a guitar follows a kora so closely you could take the two for one instrument. The kora is Sura Susso‘s, a Gambian raised in a griot family and long settled in London; the guitar is Habib Koité‘s, the Malian who tunes to a pentatonic scale and works the open strings until it sings in the kora’s register. Londi is the Mandinka word for knowledge, and Susso sings it in Mandinka and Wolof as a tribute to the djeli, the West African storytellers and historians who carry a people’s memory in performance rather than on the page. Both musicians were born to it, Koité into a noble line of Khassonké griots, Susso into a Gambian kora dynasty. The single opens Londi, a record a decade in the making. Susso and Koité met in 2016, when promoter and label African Night Fever, showcasing African music in the Brighton Area, brought Koité to Britain and put Susso on as support, and the nightly improvising that followed grew first into a friendship and then into an album. Half of it was cut in Bamako with Koité, the rest in Banjul with Susso’s band. It arrives on 9 October as African Night Fever’s debut release, with Gambian kora player Jaliba Kuyateh guesting on another track, “Yamaro”. From the studio it moves to the stage: the Manding Melody tour carries the project across nine UK dates between 22 October and 1 November, Susso leading a cross-generational band from Senegal, Mali and The Gambia, built around kora, balafon, percussion and bass. “Londi” came out as a single on 14 August. Stream “Londi” HERE The post Daily Discovery: Habib Koité & Sura Susso – Londi appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items.album: Bringing down the walls of Jericho
items.excerpt: And when they make a long blast with the ram’s horn, when you hear the sound of the trumpet, then all the people shall shout with a great shout, and the wall of the city will fall down flat… -The Book Of Joshua, Chapter 6, Verse 5 Today we’re looking at two albums featuring saxophonists whose playing could bring down the walls of Jericho. items.body: And when they make a long blast with the ram’s horn, when you hear the sound of the trumpet, then all the people shall shout with a great shout, and the wall of the city will fall down flat… -The Book Of Joshua, Chapter 6, Verse 5 Today we’re looking at two albums featuring saxophonists whose playing could bring down the walls of Jericho. Don Dietrich and Martin Escalante aren’t interested in melody in any ordinary sense of the term. You won’t find a cover of Surrey With The Fringe On Top here. They are living entirely on the very edge of what their instruments can do, skronking, screeching, howling, maybe a made-up verb with -ing on the end should go here. You won’t come away from these albums humming. But if you can find yourself in the same headspace as these musicians, you will come away from listening to this stunning, frequently shocking music exhilarated. Richard Cook and Brian Morton, in writing The Penguin Guide To Jazz, used the word “god-bothering” several times. I’m not sure they meant it as a compliment, but I take it as one. I frequently think of it when I listen to music like this. This music certainly isn’t for everyone, even among free jazz fans. But for those looking for extremity in their music, these albums are special. Dietrichs - Live Bahdu (Relative Pitch, 2026) First up is Live Bahdu by the Dietrichs. Don Dietrich, along with Jim Sauter and Donald Miller, formed the thunderous free jazz/harsh noise band Borbetomagus. Rather than sitting around trying to think of new adjectives to describe Borbetomagus, I would just urge you to check them out. They aren’t on Bandcamp, but there are many samples of their music on Youtube. (True story. I was once on a jazz open discussion group when someone wrote in asking for recommendations for music similar to Chuck Mangione. Some evil person who was not me, I swear, suggested Borbetomagus. I’ve often wondered what became of that poor listener.) Here we have Don joined by his daughter Camille Dietrich on cello. While this album has much of what you would expect from an album with Don Dietrich, Camille’s cello provides an exciting counterpoint to Don’s saxophone. She’s equally skilled at plucking and bowing, her classical music training brings moments of peace and musicality and then her desire to wreak musical mayhem takes over. Don responds and the result is some serious fire and brimstone. There’s a moment just before the 4-minute mark when there is some relative calm, and then the duo turns on a dime to create a shocking racket. The whole album is full of such surprises. Live Bahdu by Dietrichs Max Devereaux & Martin Escalante - Consequences Live! (Caresse Cassettes, 2026) And then there’s Martin Escalante. Another frequent creator of extreme sounds, Mats Gustafsson, said of Escalante: “This is the JAZZ we need! URGENT! DEDICATED! RADICAL! Unique-face-peeling-cutting-edge- and-totally-in-your-face-MF! This is ALL we need for a better living!” Who am I to argue with Mats Gustafsson, especially when he’s writing in ALL-CAPS? You might think Mats is exaggerating, but a listen to this album will tell you otherwise. Escalante, especially when he’s accompanied by a guitar, sounds punk as hell to me. I’m taken back to college days when I would crash off the walls of my dorm room screaming along to Black Flag. On this release he’s accompanied by the guitar of Max Devereaux, who manages to hold his own amid the noise and haste. He’s capable of creating his own ruckus but also quite good at providing accompaniment to Escalante on his wildest flights. At times he sounds like a rhythm section and at times he sounds like a machine gun. I wasn’t familiar with him before this album, and have been checking out his work since getting it. I hope to write more about him in the future. Consequences Live! by Max Devereaux & Martin Escalante Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook

items.body:
ENHYPEN have returned with the next chapter of their vampire story. On 21 August, the K-pop group released their eighth mini-album, THE SIN : BLISS, the second instalment in their ongoing THE SIN series. The record follows THE SIN : VANISH and continues the story of two lovers who break a taboo in vampire society and go on the run together.

At the centre of the album is lead single 'Bloody Paradise', produced by JULiA LEWiS. Blending Brazilian funk influences with raw kick drums and an infectious chorus, the track explores the freedom the lovers find in each other even as they face what could be their final moments together.

The song arrives alongside a cinematic music video partially filmed in Peru. Featuring rich colours, vintage-inspired visuals, and a wild atmosphere, the video brings the track's tale of love, danger, and freedom to life against a distinctly Latin American backdrop.

THE SIN : BLISS expands the story through its lyrics, soundscapes, and narration, with versions presented in Korean, English, Japanese, and Chinese. Actor Park Jeong Min voices the Korean narration, while actor Kenjiro Tsuda and singer Lars Huang contribute to the Japanese and Chinese versions, respectively.

Speaking at a press conference ahead of the release, JAY shared the group's confidence in the project: “We confidently call this album the best of ENHYPEN’s career.”

“We are certain it will prove worthy of our fans’ long wait,” he added.

JUNGWON echoed the sentiment, saying, “This is the record we prepared with the fewest regrets. Because we are so satisfied with the outcome, we’re stepping into this release fully confident that it will be our brightest era yet.”

The release follows ENHYPEN's BLOOD SAGA world tour, which drew more than 193,000 fans across its Latin American and U.S. legs. The group also made appearances at Campo Marte 26 in Mexico City and San Diego Comic-Con.

items.body: SIRIUS is not a soundtrack that tries to justify its existence beyond the material it was originally created for. What Noah Rosa does is to open it up as a conversation with different artists. A cold wintry tone introduces the album. A glacial wind sweeps through. The score unfolds through slow transformations with harmony moving almost imperceptibly, but it is the dialogue between Habib El Bardi’s alto saxophone and Ruiqi Wang’s voice that gives the album its emotional centre. El Bardi’s saxophone drifts in and out of the texture with carefully judged restraint, while Wang’s voice functions as another timbral presence, dissolving into the surrounding electronics. Together they create music that feels suspended. That sense of openness is no accident. In the following interview, Noah Rosa explains that he gave both performers little more than a framework within which to improvise, allowing their own personalities to shape the music. One can hear that freedom throughout the score. Rather than sounding meticulously controlled, these pieces retain a quiet unpredictability, as though they are continually discovering themselves as they unfold. The second half of the album takes the project in a different, yet entirely coherent, direction. Rosa invited four artists to create what he calls “Refractions.” The title is more than a metaphor. These are not remixes but new perspectives on the same material, each revealing something that remained latent in the original. Vaiu’s contribution is perhaps the clearest example of this philosophy. Knowing her practice, centred on “the music underneath an instant” and on voice, time and technology as collaborators, makes perfect sense of her approach. She works from within the composition, drawing attention to tiny gestures, and the act of breathing itself. The refraction by Bios Contrast & Nilotpal Das is the album’s most transformative moment. His introduction of a quiet harmonium pulse reorganises the music from within, while fragments of the original score drift in and out of focus. Nothing feels imposed. Instead, the composition reveals another possible version of itself and, in the process, goes somewhere entirely different. Ioannis Nafpliotis pushes the material further towards electroacoustic abstraction, reducing much of the score to resonance, drone and silence, before Noah Rosa himself closes the cycle with his own “Refraction.” Rather than bringing everything full circle, Rosa acknowledges the creative dialogue established by the preceding reinterpretations. His own “Refraction” expands the sonic palette, making it more luminous and harmonically warmer. The collaborative spirit of the project extends beyond the “Refractions.” Habib El Bardi, Ruiqi Wang and the three artists behind the “Refractions” are not simply invited to decorate pre-existing compositions; they become co-authors of the record. That openness seems central to Rosa’s wider practice. Across The Radiant Tower, Drawing a Circle, The Two Headed Dragon of Forgiveness and now SIRIUS, he repeatedly returns to ideas of grief, transformation and renewal. As he explains, music is both his way of processing personal experience and of engaging with the world beyond himself. By the end, SIRIUS has become a conversation. To discuss further the production process for the album we spoke directly with Noah Rosa. Sirius began as a film score, but the album expands beyond the boundaries of the film through the four “Refraction” pieces. When you revisited the material after the film’s completion, what were you hoping to discover in the source recordings, and how did the soundtrack transform once it was allowed to exist as a standalone work rather than serving the image? Working on the score with the director Jean-Bastien was such a great experience and I really admired and connected with his vision for the film. Also getting to work with talented friends is such a gift so bringing on Habib and Ruiqi made the whole process feel special. After the film did its festival run I had gotten some good feedback on the music, it received a socan award, and I enjoyed listening to it, so we talked about putting out the soundtrack. I’d never done this before as I think of my composing work as pretty separate from my solo releases and also generally think that film music works best in the context it was created for. So with this in mind, I was more interested in re-approaching the music as a new entity and bringing new life to it. There was some music we made when initially building the sound language for the film that wasn’t used in the edit that I was excited to share. The film is really beautifully minimal and we wanted to pare back the music as much as possible to leave the stillness and quiet that it needed to hit right. So I did a new mix of all the cues to make them a bit more present for this release and during this process I thought it would be interesting to see how some other artists might respond to the material as I felt the raw elements from Habib and Ruiqi held a sort of integrity, and were imbued with the emotion of the film. I’m really grateful to evo-natura for supporting this project and Ioannis for contributing a track. I’ve always felt he understood what I was trying to do with both SIRIUS and my previous release Two Headed Dragon and I’m really happy to have it be the home for these works. Across releases such as The Radiant Tower, Drawing a Circle, The Two Headed Dragon of Forgiveness, and now Sirius, there seems to be a recurring interest in grief, transformation, spirituality, and the possibility of renewal. The Radiant Tower was conceived as a mourning album and “a eulogy to the old world,” while Drawing a Circle explored cycles of collapse and endurance, and The Two Headed Dragon of Forgiveness emerged from notions of suffering, forgiveness, and rebirth. Looking back across these works, do you see them as chapters of a larger artistic inquiry, or has each release represented a distinct attempt to process a particular moment in your life? Music is really my best language for processing what’s around me and further, my way to engage with the world. So both are true, all the works are personal and integrate processes I’m going through in my personal life but they also all hopefully work towards a greater truth beyond me. I’m very interested in transformation, change is often what we both want and fear the most… but it’s happening regardless. The album is shaped by collaboration at several levels: from Habib El Bardi’s alto saxophone and Ruiqi Wang’s voice in the original score to the contributions of artists such as Vaiu, Bios Contrast & Nilotpal Das, and Ioannis Nafpliotis in the “Refractions.” What were you looking for in these collaborators, and were there aspects of the material that surprised you when filtered through other artists’ sensibilities—particularly in the richly transformative “Refraction II” by Bios Contrast & Nilotpal Das? This is definitely one of the most collaborative projects I’ve released. Ruiqi and Habib are both incredible improvisers and I really only gave them scaffolding to work within. So much of their voice and personality comes through the music and I really think of it as a shared work. For the refractions I was interested in seeing how the raw elements could be completely recontextualized into these artists’ own sound worlds. I gave very little feedback or direction for them, mostly because these artists are all just incredible, but also because I wanted to be surprised by where they took it. Bios Contrast & Nilotpal Das is an artist I’ve admired for years. The way he’s able to move between long form minimalist drone and blown out idm with it making complete sense, the visual language, and sense of humour, all make him a really exciting artist. So I had no idea what to expect from the rework and loved how it brought this constant pulse from the harmonium while different layers from the score drift in and out. Similarly, when I first heard Vaiu’s track I was blown away by how she played in the musical landscape of the score but created something completely original, weaving her voice and sensibilities into the world. One striking aspect of your work is the way environmental sound, mythology, spirituality, and political reality coexist without ever feeling forced together. Both Drawing a Circle and Sirius direct their proceeds toward Palestinian causes, while albums such as The Two Headed Dragon of Forgiveness engage deeply with place, memory, and cultural exchange. What motivates your decision to connect these releases to concrete forms of solidarity, and do you see artistic practice as having a particular ethical responsibility in moments of ongoing crisis? I guess these are just reflections of what I care about, what I’m thinking about. I’m not making enough from music to live off anyways so I have a job to support myself. Proceeds from my releases could be supplementary to me or perhaps something a little more meaningful to someone else. It can feel a bit strange attaching monetary worth to art for me, so offering it as a gift in exchange for wealth redistribution feels more in balance. I believe all art making is political, and I hope my work carries some message of compassion and solidarity. It can also be quite a selfish and individualist thing to spend all your time trying to express your interior world so I think anything we can do to offset that by reconnecting with the world is important. Apart from artistic practice, I think we as humans all have a responsibility to reduce as much suffering as we can in our short times on this earth, or at the very least try not to add more. That is what ripples into eternity. Several of your releases—including Drawing a Circle and Sirius—have donated proceeds to Palestinian initiatives such as Grassroots Al-Quds and The Sameer Project. At a time when many artists feel pressure either to remain silent or to make overt political statements, how do you think about the relationship between sound, empathy, and action? Can ambient and experimental music contribute meaningfully to solidarity, even when it contains no explicit political message? If we are scared to even speak out about the greatest injustices happening in the world, the empires have already won. No career, status marker, or opportunity is worth turning a blind eye. I think the most important thing is patient everyday resistance and it requires constant attention. That being said I think we look to artists a little too much for their politics and social stance. Someone whose job it is to dream and play make believe might not always have the most grounded worldview. I really appreciate you asking these questions, even though I might not yet have the words to fully express what they mean to me. On a good day, I believe in music’s power to connect us with the ineffable and remind us that we are all manifestations of the same unity. Other days I think we might need less poetry and more direct action.. For now I’m just trying to be a decent person and stay connected to what matters. (Gianmarco Del Re)

And then there’s the two-hour-plus runtime. Taken... The post Sarah Davachi – The Will of Tongues appeared first on The Quietus.

items.body: Nicolas Ladoux returns as IKKo with Cheerleader, a five-track release that continues his exploration of neo-industrial electronics through a distinctly European lens. Ladoux absorbs post-punk spirit into contemporary industrial frameworks Nicolas Ladoux returns as IKKo with Cheerleader, a five-track release that continues his exploration of neo-industrial electronics through a distinctly European lens. EBM traditions underpin the record, but these tracks never settle into simple nostalgia. Instead, Ladoux navigates shifting moods with a restrained confidence, allowing atmosphere and physicality to coexist. His voice is rarely treated as a conventional lead. Rather, it functions as another instrument of intent, communicating through cadence, tone and tension as much as words. Across the release, the emotional palette is painted in shades of silver, black and white, balancing mechanical precision with flashes of vulnerability. The production remains taut throughout. Pumping low-end bass rolls beneath surges of white noise, while drums land with the hard, disciplined impact of Front 242 and Nitzer Ebb-inspired rhythms. Fleeting acid figures bubble into view before dissolving back into the machinery, adding movement without distracting from the record’s industrial core. Closing duties fall to Velvet Underwear, whose remix drives the material further towards brutalist architecture, amplifying its weight and severity while preserving the original’s sense of disciplined restraint. Throughout Cheerleader, echoes of John Lydon‘s Public Image Ltd. emerge in the stark vocal phrasing and confrontational minimalism, yet Ladoux never slips into imitation. Instead, he absorbs that post-punk spirit into a contemporary industrial framework, resulting in a focused, stylish statement that understands the enduring power of tension over excess. Cheerleader is available on Roulette Rekordz. [Bandcamp] Cheerleader by IKKoThe post IKKo :: Cheerleader EP (Roulette Rekordz) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — From the very first notes of drums and piano, that fusion of classical music and avant-garde jazz is palpable; there is something here that breaks boundaries. As the trombone and saxophone join in to play their parts, the piano persists, seemingly indifferent to its surroundings, simply doing its own thing, and at times, it succeeds in reclaiming the spotlight. The composition speaks of something dramatic and serious, yet it avoids solemnity; it is something distinct. It is challenging, and just as one begins to digest it, the more jazz-oriented improvisational section arrives, bringing the electric guitar into the mix. Notes are exchanged between piano and guitar; they never stop playing and rewriting the rules, with so much happening simultaneously. This is the work of the Scottish group Graham Costello's Strata, featuring Costello himself on drums and Fergus McCreadie, whose classical training is clearly evident. And all of this was merely "Obelisk," the opening track.There is a structure they cannot escape, predetermined frameworks within which to move, perhaps mirroring humanity itself, or the modern and postmodern world: defined spaces for improvisation set against a predetermined beginning and end. For chaos to exist, order must come first.Another key aspect of tracks like "Stoic" or "96" is how their minimalism fuels a hypnotic pattern; on "96," Fergus McCreadie plays two distinct parts with both hands, effectively becoming, at times, a trio consisting of bass, drums, and two pianos. When the guitar enters, the atmosphere shifts to something almost cinematic, yet Joe Williamson also leans into repetitive patterns, subtly introducing variations within them.When "Jade" begins, with Costello providing drum accompaniment for Ferguson, I think of Keith Jarrett and his immense influence, an artist who, not coincidentally, was also deeply immersed in the classical world. However, the progressive dimension it acquires lies in the modal approach of the music, that European brand of minimalism that involves deliberately staying within a single scale for an extended period. And yet... the tension never flags, because the way they do it is something new. It is exciting and compels you to keep listening for more."Ocelot" evokes John Coltrane, another essential reference point, where Harry Weir's saxophone naturally takes the lead, at times breaking free; yet, thanks to the textures crafted by the piano and guitar, it soon evolves into something more... it becomes progressive jazz. It is a free-flowing symphony, executed to perfection in every detail, yet one that never loses sight of melody as a whole.The tonal palette that emerges when the guitar and trombone join forces to improvise recalls the best of early Chicago and Groove Collective, bands that, at times, seemed to have more members on stage than there were audience members watching them. Graham Costello and his band evoke the best of that era with an unmistakable timeless quality that keeps them eternally relevant.At times, the track "Sole" feels like an exercise in illustrating what it would sound like to hear sand falling in an hourglass, slow, almost imperceptible at first, then rapid and resounding as little remains toward the end. Fergus McCreadie's notes know just when to intelligently appeal to emotion and strike a deep chord; "Sapphire", meanwhile, reminded me of Morphine in its use of wind instruments with a dark, rock-tinged edge, while the piano provides accompaniment until an almost Baltic melody emerges.The cover promises a multitude of textures interwoven in a way that is modern, chaotic, yet cohesive... though that black-and-white imagery doesn't quite capture the inherent feeling, which doesn't always need to be stated explicitly. "Fly," the final track, features repetitive loops reminiscent of Stereolab alongside trombonist Steve Turre playing conch shells... yet the drums cut through, stamping the track with their own rhythm. Is it Noise rock? Post-rock? It is all of that combined with jazz, and because it blends all these elements, it becomes something distinct. It is a form of jazz that evolves and mutates, and for that very reason, it remains alive.
