items.body: Review by BrufordFreak — With everybody on board employing electric or amplified sound what we have here is some true Jazz-Rock Fusion (of the Herbie Hancock Mwandishi school of influence). The album's material (of all original Don Harris compositions) was recorded on November 17 and 18, 1970, at MPS Tonstudio in Villingen, Germany, and then released soon thereafter (probably in early 1971).WARNING: This is really a Don "Sugar Cane" Harris album: Volker Kriegel is just a collaborating guest; all song compositions are credited solely to Don Harris.1. "Keep On Driving" (4:05) music solidly rooted in Blues and Blues-Rock traditions on which Volker and Sugar Cane take turns presenting the "Proud Mary"-like main melody and their variations and improvisational interpretations thereof. Already one can sense how dextrously-talented Volker is. John Taylor must be playing an early version of an electric piano as it sounds quite odd (and primitive). The rhythmatists are playing something quite basic and simplistic, following the main melody line quite closely, which feels rather amateurish. (8.75/10)2. "Blues On The Moon" (6:53) unstructured bass play with virtually solo violin improvising some melody over the top while John, Volker, and Tony Oxley play with experimental sound-making from behind the scenes. Toward the fourth minute the bass, drums, and electric piano start to gel into some kind of loose three-chord vamp as Sugar Cane continues exploring his own bluesy melody line. The song begins to deconstruct and bottom out slowly almost from the five-minute mark on with no one else really getting much solo time, everybody just kind of loosely jamming to that three-chord vamp. (13.125/15)3. "Which Way Is The Bathroom?" (4:02) electric violin begins soloing Jean-Luc Ponty-like from the opening note over two-chord electric piano, bass, and touch-drive drums, switching the rhythm track a bit in the second minute as Sugar Cane peaks. Volker enters in the second half of the second minute, truly ripping a few jaw-dropping slurring shred-lines before giving up the spotlight first to John Taylor, then Tony Oxley, before Sugar Cane returns in the fourth minute to take back the lead, rhythm section slowing down and spacing things out a bit as Sugar Cane really flies. Then the song is slowly faded out. (8.875/10)4. "Desiree" (8:40) a slower paced, cool spacious jazz motif that sounds inspired by the old Miles Kind of Blue album while the piano has gone electric, the bass, too, and the melodic violin is also electrified. I really like the way Tony Oxley's drums are recorded: nice full toms and crisp, clear cymbals. The only other soloist on the song is John Taylor on his electric piano; Volker is absent from this one. A nice, laid-back tune that offers nice solos but nothing jaw-dropping or ground-breaking. (17.667/20)5. "Almost Broke" (5:58) electric piano play from John Taylor sounds like a Vibraphone, the amazing bass play is Sugar Cane! Which means multiple tracks were used in recording this one. Volker gets some nice solo time but really has little contributions otherwise: it's mostly Don, John, and drummer Tom Oxley performing as the rhythm trio with Volker and Sugar Cane taking some turns with electric guitar and electric violin, respectively. (9/10)6. "Coitus Interruptus" (4:58) Mississippi Swamp Blues with Volker playing rhythm with Sugar Cane's bass while Cane's wah-wah-treated electric violin presents the bluesy main melody from the opening note (sounding a bit like a dobro!) Cool sound! Volker takes over the lead around 1:50 with some raunchy distortion and overdrive adding a stinky stank to his solo (and the music). John Taylor is next, his also-stinky distorted electric piano is mixed in an odd left-back position (opposite Volker). A little flashiness from Tony precedes Sugar Cane's re-entry with his squawky violin. Kind of a cool sound despite its very rudimentary blues construction. (8.875/10)7. "Remember The Past" (10:08) again John Taylor's jazzy Herbie Hancock-like electric piano play coupled with Don's slow-struttin' bass and Tony's excellent spacious drum play give Sugar Cane the chance to really spill his guts with his treated electric and acoustic violins. Volker doesn't really make his presence known until the fourth minute: once Cane has finished his first extended solo. Volker's solo is pretty standard jazz guitar until he starts shred-bending his guitar strings as if he were Sonny Sharrock, Chris Spedding, Pete Townsend, or Roye Albrighton. Then John gets a turn, occupying the seventh minute before some guitar scratching signals time for a bass solo (during which Volker continues to play with the feedback effects on his electric guitar). The band comes back to the opening theme for the final minute as Sugar Cane closes things up with his plaintive melody (while Volker and/or Tony continue to play with electronically-induced sound effects). Kind of cool experimental stuff within some laid-back down-home front porch smooth jazz. (17.75/20)Total Time 44:44I am definitely surprised by how little Volker Kriegel's contributions are considered: he's mostly there to provide solos only--often very brief ones at that. In contrast, I'm also surprised by the how much creative input drummer Tony Oxley and electric pianist John Taylor are given. And, lastly, who knew that Don Harris was such a bass player (and composer)?! B/four stars; a solid contribution of early experimental Jazz-Rock Fusion.

items.album: VOLKER KRIEGEL With a Little Help from My Friends (Jazz Rock/Fusion, 1968)
items.excerpt: Review by BrufordFreak — One of those Renaissance men that could have found success in many (any?) careers, this album was Volker's debut as a band leader. After stints with Ingfreid Hoffmann and Klaus Doldinger in the mid-60s, for With a Little Help from My Friends we find the creative guitarist working with some of the same musicians that he worked with on Klaus Doldinger's Goes On album while also working with drummer Peter Baumeister for the first time. Tracks A1 to A4 were recorded in
items.body: Review by BrufordFreak — One of those Renaissance men that could have found success in many (any?) careers, this album was Volker's debut as a band leader. After stints with Ingfreid Hoffmann and Klaus Doldinger in the mid-60s, for With a Little Help from My Friends we find the creative guitarist working with some of the same musicians that he worked with on Klaus Doldinger's Goes On album while also working with drummer Peter Baumeister for the first time. Tracks A1 to A4 were recorded in 1968 in K�ln while Tracks B1 to B3 were recorded in 1968 in Frankfurt. The album was then released by Liberty Records, also sometime in 1968. ‎A1. "With A Little Help From My Friends" (3:13) though quite faithful to the Beatles' original vocal melody lines, Volker is so accurate and precise as to almost seem reverential (i.e., not the creative Jazz treatment I was expecting). (8.875/10)A2. "Blues For Instance" (5:10) definitely built/based on American Blues construct and melodies, Volker, bassist Peter Trunk, and drummer Cees See give ample life to this original composition. Not my favorite type of music, but the trio really bring their best to make it both interesting and impressive. (8.75/10)A3. "Norwegian Wood" (2:20) now this is more of what I was expecting from Volker's first tackle of a Lennon & McCartney tune: creative interpretation, juxtaposition, variation, and improvisation galore; he's using the original as a jumping off point, not as a template to follow respectfully close. The injections of Jazz twists and turns are rampant and replete--and nary a sitar or sitar-imitation necessary! (9/10)A4. "Traffic Jam" (3:59) the fourth and final song from the K�ln studio recording sessions finds Volker stretching out with his band on this original composition that is founded in more of a folk Jazz tradition similar to the works of Django Rheinhard but Volker finds his usual ways of making it his own: expanding Django-like phrasing into American Jazz traditions pioneered by Charlie Christian as well as sneaking in a some flourishes of psychedelic rock into the last minute of the song. This, to my mind, is the first song that really begins to show Volker's wildly creative genius in tandem with his virtuosic dexterity. I really like drummer Cees See's instinctual sensibilities and control when he fully joins in around the halfway mark. (8.875/10)B1. "Morandi" (3:29) another Kriegel original that finds Volker exploring the sounds and styles of Spanish classical guitaring of Rodrigo, Segovia, Ni�o Ricardo, and Manolo Sanl�car. Most people think of Volker as an electric guitarist but I'm here to tell you that he was an amazing acoustic guitarist as well. As I suggested in this review's introductory paragraph, I consider Volker quite the eclectic musician: a Zelig who could and would transgress fearlessly into any style or genre of sound or music with an ease that I credit to intuition as much as to intention--and the dude was totally self-taught! (9.125/10)B2. "Na Na Imboro" (8:42) a composition from Claudio Szenkar, the Vibraphonist sitting in on all of the songs on Side Two (those songs recorded in Frankfurt). The main melody and structure have quite a similar feel to the song "Mas Que Nada" (made famous internationally in 1966 by Sergio Mendes & Brasil '66). While Peter Baumeister flails away with great vim and vigor, bassist G�nter Lenz keeps up as Claudio and Volker trade vibrant and dynamic solos, both challenging the other to up their game, even urging the other on from beneath the soloist's spotlight while the other is soloing! Very cool and energetic Jazz! Virtuosi, both! (18.625/20)B3. "Interpunctuation" (4:44) though Claudio and Volker lay down the chords, this song presents itself as more of a vehicle to show off the drumming talents of Peter Baumeister. After the first minute, though, Peter and G�nter settle into something structured while Volker nad Claudio take turns soloing, Volker riffing with such smooth fluidity as to surprise and astonish, over and over again. Claudio uses his genius to show his chord play during his solo (toward the end). I kind of wish Peter's drums were mixed a little more quietly into the final mix: they can be a little overbearing. (9.125/10)Total time 31:37Though for whatever reason I find myself resistant to listening to Volker Kriegel material, I always come away super impressed by this musician's abilities. He attacks the guitar with such intuition and virtuosity and yet he somehow makes it sound so easy! There are other fluid guitarists out there but I can think of no other who makes his fluid movements and clear note play seem as effortless as Volker--even here, at age 25, in this, his first record as a bandleader. And then there's the factor of his compositional abilities: these four original compositions of his are so good, so complete, and so confident, that it makes the listener swear that they must be covers of old classic songs by much more mature and practiced composers! A-/five stars; a minor masterpiece of proto-Jazz-Rock Fusion: here fusing jazz interpretations of a variety of musics (Pop, Spanish, American Blues, and Brasilian) with eclectic meanderings from his encyclopedic mind. Brilliant! Volker is a force! And I need to hear more of Claudio Szenkar's work!

items.body: Review by alainPP — Castanarc's sound initially evokes Genesis and Yes, then Marillion, with a touch of Saga and a good deal of Pallas, for this sixth album of symphonic soft prog rock."Forged by the Sun," the eponymous track, features neo-classical keyboards and Yes-esque 80s-style backing vocals. A catchy, driving keyboard provides the basic rhythm, while Mark delivers his distinctive vocals. The catchy, crowd-pleasing track features a beautiful ambient section starting at 5:30, a blend of languor and sweetness against a backdrop of Yes. The break then flirts with Camel-like keyboards midway through, venturing into the symphonic-ambient realm of Marillion's heyday, even hinting at Vangelis's new age. Crystal-clear piano and vocals reminiscent of Collins and Pallas languidly follow, culminating in a moving guitar riff that exudes an ethereal symphonic quality."Ceasefire for the Innocent" is a Genesis-esque melody reminiscent of the 70s, with a velvety organ and vocals definitively on Collins. An easy ballad that unfolds with Neil's juicy guitar solo at its heart; the ambient, jazzy-bluesy finale lingers, perfectly progressive with its velvety atmosphere. Watery notes in the purest nu-metal tradition, a bit more repetitive than the opening track. "Cue Rain" is a marshmallow ballad?those who know what I mean will understand: whispered vocals, ethereal piano, and romantic acoustics hinting at a US country vibe. Mark loves Phil Collins, David is at ease with his melting keyboards, and Dave Holley's crystalline guitar guest invites you to put your arms around each other and dance around the progressive table.Castanarc improves with age like certain drinks; a beautiful album navigating between the 80s and today without a whiff of imitation. (4,5)

items.album: JACK BRUCE Songs For A Tailor (Jazz Rock/Fusion, 1969)
items.excerpt: Review by BrufordFreak — The highly-revered bass player's first solo album release finds Jack supported in part by members of Colosseum (Dick Heckstall-Smith and Jon Hiseman), in part Nucleus (Chris Spedding and drummer John Marshall). Bruce was, of course, a former member of Cream (with guitarist Eric Clapton and drummer Ginger Baker), Manfred Mann, John Mayall's Bluesbreakers (with Eric Clapton), and both the Graham Bond Organization (with Baker and Heckstall-Smith) and Graham Bond Quart
items.body: Review by BrufordFreak — The highly-revered bass player's first solo album release finds Jack supported in part by members of Colosseum (Dick Heckstall-Smith and Jon Hiseman), in part Nucleus (Chris Spedding and drummer John Marshall). Bruce was, of course, a former member of Cream (with guitarist Eric Clapton and drummer Ginger Baker), Manfred Mann, John Mayall's Bluesbreakers (with Eric Clapton), and both the Graham Bond Organization (with Baker and Heckstall-Smith) and Graham Bond Quartet (with Baker and guitarist John McLaughlin) as well as Alexis Korner's Blues Incorporated (his first collaboration with Baker and Heckstall-Smith). The material that became Songs for a Tailor was recorded in London in April and May of 1969 and then released in Britain by Polydor Records on August 29 of 1969 (Oct. 6 in the States by ATCO). 1. "Never Tell Your Mother She's Out of Tune" (3:41) R&B Brass Rock with a complex syncopated construction that uses dissonant chords from both the horn section as well as an unusual progression for the odd vocal melody to sing over. The drumming is particularly tight but it's the horn arrangements that really knock your socks off. Jack's bass playing is impressive, especially toward the end when he starts to stray outside the main riff he created to found the song over. Not a great nor memorable song except for the unusual horn arrangements. (8.875/10)2. "Theme for an Imaginary Western" (3:30) sounding like a PROCOL HARUM song with both vocal melody, band's chord progression, organ and piano dominance, and pace, Jack's voice has a kind of jazzy VAN MORRISON quality and styling to it. Another okay song. (8.75/10)3. "Tickets to Water Falls" (3:00) a brief piano intro turns into another unusual jazzy song with a bit of a Caribbean flavor to it despite its loud free-flowing Jazz-Rock bass and multiple keyboards and spicy rhythm guitar (which Chris Spedding later turns into a bit of a George Harrison-like solo). Very interesting. (8.875/10)4. "Weird of Hermiston" (2:24) a Blues-Rock based song that again crosses into that area of music that is more commonly traversed by artists like Van Morrison, The Band, Jethro Tull, and George Harrison--this might even be considered proto-Americana! (8.75/10)5. "Rope Ladder to the Moon" (2:54) a Blues-Rock song that sounds very much like it could have come from one of JETHRO TULL's earliest albums. I like this one. Even the vocal sounds as quirky and adventurous as something Ian Anderson (or Van Morrison) would do. (8.875/10)6. "The Ministry of Bag" (2:49) this one is pure Memphis Blues--as if Booker T & The M.G.'s and The Memphis Horns are on board from start to finish. Jack's singing is aggressive and bluesy like young Dr. John or Wilson Pickett. A top three song. (9/10)7. "He the Richmond" (3:36) Jack's strumming acoustic guitar opens this where he is joined by John Marshall's drums and his own bass while singing a vocal as if channelling a combination of Richie Havens, Ian Anderson, and Dr. John. The uncredited harmonizing vocals of the second minute are really unusual--and cool! A top three song for me. (9/10)8. "Boston Ball Game 1967" (1:45) loud horns and pounding piano dominate this one so much that Jack's multiple vocal(s) tracks are nearly drowned out (and seem to have to force themselves to be heard). Kind of cool but could've been turned into something more. (Or else.) (4.375/5)9. "To Isengard" (5:28) acoustic guitars strumming and picking while multiple vocal lines are tracking--the lead using a delicate, high-pitched timbre (that sounds like Rod Stewart trying to sing up high). Very interesting. I really like the vocal harmonies as well as the interplay between Jack and Chris' two guitars. At 3:15 there is a brief stop out of which explodes a uptempo motif that spreads things out among bass, drums, and the psychedelic sound creations and play of Chris Spedding's electric guitar. While I prefer the first half, I did enjoy the second half, too. My final top three song. (8.875/10)10. "The Clearout" (2:35) trying to go back to the Cream world? Heavy power chords from both electric guitar and bass over Jon Hiseman's Ginger Baker-like militaristic drumming. Not my favorite use of these talented artist's skills. And I didn't even mention the Roger Daltry-like singing or lyrics over the Beatles' "Birthday"-like melody line. (8.75/10)Total time 31:42Jack can certainly impress with his bass playing--as if he could be the father of Jaco Pastorius--but his active and jazzy lines (and sound) are not always as fitting to the music and his vocal stylings and lyrics aren't quite the kind of stuff for the AM charts. B/four stars; while I definitely appreciate the uniqueness of Jack's talents and vision, I find most of the music on this album to be almost confusing and messy, and the lyrics to be nearly impregnable and, probably, written from a very personal, albeit creative perspective (not unlike those of Van Morrison).

items.album: BLOOD SWEAT AND TEARS Blood, Sweat and Tears (Jazz Rock/Fusion, 1969)
items.excerpt: Review by BrufordFreak — Exit founder and leader Al Kooper (turning toward the production and A&R side of Columbia Records), here today is power vocalist David Clayton-Thomas. Other members remaining from the debut album include the excellent rhythm corps of bassist Jim Fielder, drummer Bobby Colomby, and guitarist Steve Katz as well as sax player Fred Lipsius and trombonist Dick Halligan (who now has added piano, flute, and organ to his The album was recorded in New York City at Columbia'
items.body: Review by BrufordFreak — Exit founder and leader Al Kooper (turning toward the production and A&R side of Columbia Records), here today is power vocalist David Clayton-Thomas. Other members remaining from the debut album include the excellent rhythm corps of bassist Jim Fielder, drummer Bobby Colomby, and guitarist Steve Katz as well as sax player Fred Lipsius and trombonist Dick Halligan (who now has added piano, flute, and organ to his The album was recorded in New York City at Columbia's 30th Street Studios ("The Church") during the span of October 7-22, 1968 and then released at the end of the year from where it dominated the charts, holding the #1 spot for six weeks in 1969, spawning three hit singles to each reach #2: "You've Made Me So Very Happy," "Spinning Wheel," and "And When I Die" before winning the 1970 Grammy Award for Album of the Year.1. "Variations On A Theme By Erik Satie (1st and 2nd Movements)" * (2:30) performed rather faithfully by Steve Katz providing the chords normally left to the piano's left hand on his classical guitar with flutes, and/or recorders tracking the main melody up top--until, that is, until the tinkling of a percussionists winde chimes signals a bridge to a fully meted out Brass Rock version (the "2nd Movement") varying the notes and chords with highly-treated (flanged) drums, bass, and loud horn section. Interesting! (9.125/10)2. "Smiling Phases" (5:10) a song that really puts on full display the band's power and enthusiastic energy while also introducing their powerful new vocalist, David Clayton-Thomas. After 90 seconds, the band launches into an impressive jazzy instrumental section in which bass player Jim Fielder, drummer Bobby Colomby show their skills as the horns and Fred Lipsius' piano show off their skills over what turns out to be a two-part movement: the first fast, the second slow and protracted, before returning to the opening motif for David and the band to finish with the same energy as they opened with to bookend the song. Nice! (9/10)3. "Sometimes In Winter "(3:08) smooth, beautiful, fully-orchestrated music with the smooth vocal of Steve Katz, the band finds themselves creating more of that Jimmy Webb folkie, anachronistic Baroque Pop that is so pleasing to the ear. I like this song very much. Steve Katz could definitely have had a career as a singer: he sounds like a cross between a certain member of The Association and Bobby Darren. (9.25/10)4. "More and More" (3:04) picking up where "Smiling Phases" left off (though David's voice is mixed a little more deeply into the soundscape than before). More creative uses for the horn section to inject their accents into the mix (substituting for the B.B. King-like blues guitar riffs). Jim and Bobby bring it with such amazing energy and skill! The futuristic (Frippian) guitar tone used by Steve Katz in the solo toward the end of the second minute, during the organ-based instrumental mid-section, is quite cool (and loud)! Incredibly tight and powerful musicianship on this complex tune. (9.125/10)5. "And When I Die" (4:05) the hit cover of Laura Nyro's song, the song is notable for its dynamic shift between its sparse, dirge-like harmonica opening, the ensuing easy-going circus-music-like verses and the way the music turns to vaudeville-Western-showtune-like as they go on. And then there are the dramatically-held suspension of the song's title in the chorus and unusual pauses. Very much like something one would see on a Broadway musical. The faithful rendering of a rather complicated composition is the most impressive part for me (on a song that I've never really been very high on). (9/10)6. "God Bless The Child" (5:56) another song that feels stage-worthy (which makes sense since it was composed by Arthur Herzog, Jr. and Billie Holiday). In a very interesting (and totally unexpected) twist, at 3:06 the song turns into a Afro-Cubano-flavored piano- and percussion-based jam for the horn players to really stretch out: both collectively and each, individually. But then at 4:24 the song comes back to its origins (though with noticeably more forceful horns, more organ, and the joinder of a bluesy harmonica, which weren't so prevalent in the opening). Ballsy but these guys are definitely up to the challenge. (9.125/10)7. "Spinning Wheel" (4:07) one of those memorable brainworm songs, this one composed by newcomer David Clayton-Thomas. The horns were always my favorite part though David is solid (and even able to show some sensitivity). Definitely the most interchangeable song with the other Brass Rock pioneer, CHICAGO (Transit Authority). The instrumental section in the middle (which is sometimes cut out for radio play) is pretty cool--as is the finale with it's horn blasts, great drumming, and calliope-like recorder play. (9/10)8. "You've Made Me So Very Happy" (4:19) the album's first single release, it was borrowed from the Motown catalogue having been covered by one of its authors, Brenda Holloway in a mildly-successful 1967 release as a 45 rpm single (the final arrangement of which Ms. Holloway fought hard to control, a battle she ultimately lost--which led to her leaving Motown/Tamla). BS&T's version was a massive chart topper that remains memorable and emotionally relevant to this day. I am most impressed by David Clayton-Thomas' ability to tone it down and soften his delivery for the tender, sensitive verses. (9.25/10)9. "Blues-Part II" (11:45) an instrumental epic that opens with organ, bass, drums, all of which are quite simple and rudimentary (which is greatly disappointing considering the absolutely jaw-dropping skills the band's rhythm section has shown in the super-tight, super demanding arrangements of all their vocal songs). By the time the fifth minute rolls around the band has finally settled into something more meaty (though, ironically, it's a two-chord vamp) over which Fred Lipsius performs a long multi-part solo on his alto sax: at first over the fast-tempo vamp but then equally-impactful over the slowed down for the seventh and eighth minutes. How humorous is it that the band (Jim Fielder) chooses the "Sunshine of Your Love"/"In-a-gadda-da-vida" bass line to open and carry the next section. Luckily, he lets go of it at 8:40, whereupon the band transitions into a purely-Blues motif over which David sings in a genuinely-feeling blues tradition as Steve Katz tries to project a Blues guitar tone and style while Bobby bashes away on the drum kit beneath and the horn section slowly ramps up their intensity--until someone in the production booth decided to pull the plug: they slowly fade the song out even while David is launching into a classic Wilson Pickett lyric with increasing power and emotion! (22/25)10. "Variations On A Theme By Erik Satie (1st Movement)" * (1:37) a replication of the opening movement from the beginning of the album, this time ending before the Brass Rock rendering starts--with the sound of a door slamming shut! (4.75/5)* Adapted from Satie's "Trois Gymnop�dies"Total time 45:41A-/five stars; a minor masterpiece of genre-leading Brass Rock. Though I am nowhere near as much a fan of this album as their debut, I recognize the superior craftsmanship that went into the rendering of each and every song and cannot imagine denying it it's deserved masterpiece status.

items.body: To complement her interview in The Wire 511, Korean American composer Lucy Liyou creates an exclusive Wire mix Lucy Liyou grew up in Seattle, and as a child was a talented classical pianist. Her strengths, at first, were late Romantic and 20th century music; then she discovered the likes of Andrew Hill and Cecil Taylor, which inform the fiendishly difficult piano figures in her latest album Mr Cobra. Mr Cobra allowed Liyou to explore these influences, alongside her many others, including updated Korean folk opera, horror, vocality, narrative, maximalism, and families. This mix of Liyou's influences and inspirations was compiled exclusively for The Wire. Sharon Udoh “Great Is Thy Faithfulness” Cheryl E Leonard “moffen” Phew & Danielle de Picciotto “The Cat” more eaze “the producer” Blue Gene Tyranny “She Wore Red Shoes” Marran Gosov “Eifersucht” Borana Ramizi “Dying Is The Color Yellow” Iris Our “Splits and Wants” Lucy Liyou with Nick Zanca “Live in Paris February 2024” Samuel Beckett (performed by Billie Whitelaw) “Not I (1973)” Read Hugh Morris’s full interview with Lucy Liyou in The Wire 511. items.body: There comes a point, after enough headlines, alerts, feeds, clips, corrections, denials, cropped videos, expert panels, anonymous sources, and professional faces staring gravely into cameras, when information begins to resemble an industrial solvent poured directly onto the brain. Reality remains somewhere underneath, presumably, but reaching it requires digging through so many layers of interpretation that certainty starts feeling less like knowledge than another product somebody is trying to sell. Baltimore electro-industrial duo Pygmy Children, brothers Pete and Brian Roper, plant Proof in Lies directly inside that psychic mess. The track leads their forthcoming fifth studio album, Into The Silence. The music carries the physical force of industrial rock without turning itself into machinery: drums strike with hard, deliberate weight, guitars grind against serrated electronics, and Pete Roper delivers his vocals from somewhere between accusation, exhaustion, and the suspicion that everyone in the room has already agreed upon the wrong version of events. Nine Inch Nails, Ministry, Christian Death, and the severe electronic rock of later Gary Numan all come to mind, although Pygmy Children funnel those affinities through their own Baltimore-bred sense of unease. “I rediscovered some old lyrics in a notebook for a track that had never fully materialized,” says Pete Roper. “I still remembered the original chord progression, so I rewrote the lyrics, recorded the initial drum tracks, and the project began to take shape.” That resurrection feels appropriate for a song preoccupied with evidence, memory, and the slippery authority of whatever appears before our eyes. Proof in Lies examines a culture in which perception competes continuously with experience, while repetition can make the grotesque seem ordinary and the ridiculous seem plausible. Once violence becomes entertainment, catastrophe becomes content, and human suffering becomes another image between advertisements, the ability to distinguish participation from spectatorship begins to rot. Roper ultimately locates his remaining point of orientation in music, describing it as a place of clarity, peace, and honest expression. That conviction gives the track an emotional center beneath its metal-edged pressure: somewhere behind all the competing signals remains the stubborn belief that expression can still communicate something uncorrupted. The accompanying video pushes the idea further through live performance footage, original visual effects, and public-domain animation produced during the 1940s, recombined into an uneasy collision of obedience, fantasy, violence, and entertainment. “The imagery in the video challenges our blurred perception of the boundary between reality and fantasy as we move through life increasingly disconnected from one another, following established paths without question and becoming desensitized to experiences beyond ourselves. The social acceptance of violence as a form of entertainment also emerges as a recurring theme. Finally, the unanswered question of what the recurring mysterious character possesses invites deeper interpretation.” Watch below: By the end, Proof in Lies leaves certainty battered beyond recognition, which may be the most accurate portrait possible of an age where everybody has access to everything and somehow nobody can agree on what they have seen. Listen to Proof In Lies below and order the single here, out now via Re:Mission Entertainment. items.body: Death has always had a public-relations problem. We prefer it announced by thunder, church bells, skeletal hands, or some other unmistakable emblem, because ambiguity would require us to admit how easily extinction can borrow the language of consolation. On We’re Here, Washington, D.C., duo 2DCAT writes entirely from the perspective of the dead, addressing those who remain alive. On first listen, their message can sound warm: you are not alone, someone is present, and your fear will eventually lift. That reading is intentional, since 2DCAT imagines it as what the dead themselves would want us to hear. Yet the speakers from beyond the grave offer no promise of survival. They are here because they have already died, joining the largest congregation imaginable: everyone who came before us. “Fate sealed. Gates closed. A door appears. The path looks clear.” The verses trace a single account of dying, with each image marking another irreversible step. This sequence offers no metaphor for hope, recovery, or passage into a brighter phase. The dead recognize the path because they have already walked it and know where it leads. Their assurance that fear will soon be gone refers to what happens afterward, when fear disappears along with the life experiencing it. HAEZL, an opera singer whose disciplined voice gives the words an eerie composure, sings as one of those departed voices without the theatrical menace one might expect. Her restraint is essential. Death here has no need to raise its voice. Johan Hauck builds and fabricates the synthesizers used on the track, a detail that gives the music an unusually physical provenance. These machines are handmade objects producing music about the disappearance of bodies, and their cool contours provide an elegant counterweight to HAEZL’s formal poise. The arrangement draws from early European synthpop and darkwave, favoring severe textures, measured motion, and a sense of space that seems to narrow as the song proceeds. The chorus—“We’re here to remind you you’re never alone”—embodies a literal truth. Everyone who experienced the same ending still exists within this collective voice, surrounding the living as part of an immense community. The dead have always been present, and the living are simply a fleeting minority within that ongoing presence. Their companionship is genuine, not menacing: having shared the same fear, they provide the reassurance that comes from understanding how every life ultimately concludes. The video presses that claustrophobia further. Near-black frames, unstable illumination, and coarse grain reduce the visible world to fragments, as though the image itself were losing access to ordinary life. Faces and forms seem caught at the edge of perception, suspended between the unseen multitude speaking through the song and those still able to hear them. The result is less a ghost story than an encounter with inevitability, stripped of folklore and made strangely intimate. “We wouldn’t blame anyone for hearing this as hopeful,” says Hauck. “The gates being steeled, the door appearing, the path looking clear… that’s not hope. That’s dying. The dead are your guides because they’ve already made that walk.” Watch the video for We’re Here below: We’re Here belongs to a series of recent singles from 2DCAT’s forthcoming, still-unannounced album, mapping a world in collapse through several human positions: those waiting for salvation that never arrives, those retreating inward when the burden becomes unbearable, and those whose anger accelerates the destruction they fear. We’re Here supplies the voice of those who have already passed through that world. They look back upon the people still living inside it with the terrible clarity of knowing exactly how it ends. The release follows 2DCAT’s first German tour, which included dates in Leipzig, München, Berlin, and Köln’s Echoes of Rebellion festival, carrying this communion between the living and the dead into crowded rooms abroad. The We’re Here EP is out now. Order here. items.body: We’ll spread open to spread across the sky and I’ll take you with me on the day I die There are songs about temptation that behave like sermons, warning you about the cliff while quietly admiring the view, and then there are numbers like Staytus’s Secret Hand, which grabs desire by the collar, drags it under the lights, and asks why anybody should pretend the danger isn’t part of the attraction. Sam Grundemann has built Staytus around the place where industrial rock, electronic abrasion, metal weight, and theatrical self-invention start elbowing one another for room, and this track makes the collision physical. Secret Hand is thick with tasty bass, hard guitar, and electronic pressure, but the arrangement has enough space for every hit to register. The riffs land with the blunt pleasure of machinery being overclocked, while Grundemann’s voice moves between invitation and warning as though those impulses have been caught sharing the same bloodstream. Desire here has teeth. Power changes hands every few seconds. Submission becomes less a conclusion than a wager placed with full knowledge of the odds. “Secret Hand has some of my favorite guitar and bass work I’ve done,” said Staytus. “I wanted the music to feel just as seductive as it is dangerous—something that pulls you in before you realize how intense it has become. The video gave me the opportunity to fully embody that energy and step into this fearless, unapologetic version of myself as an artist.” The setting also folds back into the song’s title. Secret Hand was recorded at Secret Hand Studios in Los Angeles, owned by drummer Jeff Friedl, and Staytus has described the place as central to the track’s creation. The music cheekily treats the phrase as something far more illicit and suggestive than a studio name. Lyrically, Secret Hand navigates between caution and desire, craving to strengthen a drunken friendship despite potential regret and instability. Its vivid imagery combines themes of sex, pain, ambition, and exploitation, while the recurring “fuck the band” chorus hints at a clandestine alliance aimed at gaining advantage. That tension becomes even clearer in Vicente Cordero’s video, which traps Staytus inside a black room streaked with neon, fog rolling through the frame while the camera churns around her in visual delirium. There is little distance between performer and viewer. Grundemann occupies the frame like somebody testing how much voltage a body can carry before performance turns into possession. Hair, leather, light, movement, smoke: Cordero keeps tightening the frame until the room feels less like a set than a pressure chamber. The best part of the video is how thoroughly she commits to that embodiment. Nothing is coy, and nothing needs an alibi. Grundemann looks at the camera with the confidence of somebody who knows spectacle can be both armor and confession, then lets the song’s menace do the rest. Secret Hand turns appetite into performance, and risk into the sort of pleasure where the warning label is part of the invitation. items.body: Freedom is not the same as improvement, because freedom concerns our relationship to what happens, not merely the circumstances themselves. A prison can be renovated and still remain a prison in the mind. When suffering has organized your habits, loyalties, and sense of self, its removal may feel strangely like a loss. Anger often outlives the conditions that produced it because the body keeps yesterday’s argument alive. So when life improves, there is no commandment that says gratitude must arrive immediately. Sometimes liberation begins with allowing the old anger to exhaust itself, until you discover you no longer need it. There is something peculiarly German about naming a post-punk record Kleinkunst, a word usually reserved for cabaret, small-stage performance, and other modest forms of cultural production, then filling it with the psychic debris of cities built for industries that have vanished. Mottek87 comes from Duisburg, where structural change is hardly an abstraction. Zbigniew F. and Jürgen W., longtime friends of Polish descent, formed the duo in 2024 after an evening of drinking beer and listening to records somehow turned into the decision to make one themselves. Their music has retained something of that unceremonious beginning: guitars, bass, programmed drums, sparse synthesizers, and German lyrics delivered with the plainspoken severity of people suspicious of excessive decoration. The three songs on Kleinkunst: the title track, Oszillation, and Widerstand, concern a particular kind of estrangement, in which a person remains in the same place while everything that once made the place intelligible begins to vanish. Streets endure, buildings survive, names remain attached to maps, yet the internal coordinates have shifted. Mottek87 understand that structural change is experienced privately before it becomes a statistic. One person sees cleaner air and redevelopment; another sees an entire vocabulary of work, class, habit, and belonging becoming obsolete. The music keeps that anger on a short leash. Prominent guitars recall Escape with Romeo and Pink Turns Blue, while the rhythm section has the economical discipline associated with early German post-punk and the sterner corners of Neue Deutsche Welle. Jürgen W.’s vocals lend the songs a dry Ruhr directness, carrying alienation without theatrical anguish. The arrangements leave considerable open space, which makes every bass movement and guitar phrase feel unusually exposed. Standout track Widerstand in particular has a rousing, sing-song chorus channeling Interpol. Emotional intelligence sprouts from tension. Blossoms appear where dust once gathered, lungs clear, and the protective armor accumulated over decades becomes increasingly cumbersome. Improvement carries its own insult when it arrives after the world that required such protection has already been dismantled. “Kleinkunst is about realizing that change is not automatically freedom,” says the band. “Sometimes something gets better, and you still need time to stop being angry about it.” Mottek87 record in a downtown Duisburg apartment with the shutters deliberately closed, sealing themselves off from the city they are attempting to understand. The method suits Kleinkunst. Resistance, in Mottek87’s hands, becomes less a heroic posture than an old reflex whose usefulness has become uncertain: a form of emotional muscle memory inherited from a place that keeps changing faster than its people can decide what they are prepared to surrender. Listen to Kleinkunst below and order the EP here. items.body: Hot gun, our promise bleeds You would never stop looking for me Have we left it all behind? Is it lust that’s holding the line? Intimacy becomes especially cruel once its gestures outlive the feeling that gave them meaning. A touch continues out of habit, desire reports for duty, and two people repeat the same private choreography while looking through each other as if they have never met. “Sex Machines,” the latest single from Dutch brothers Ruben and Matthijs Pol, occupies that bleakly comic interval, where lust keeps the body busy after the relationship has already vacated the premises. Following a single launch show during Paris Fashion Week in June, Pol now give that estrangement a public face in the song’s official video, directed by fashion photographer and filmmaker Rémi Lamandé. The duo treats New Wave as a living language, bringing music, fashion, moving image, and performance into the same sharpened frame. Here, a lovers’ closed loop becomes a roving interview program whose strangers seem to know every private detail. The song advances on twitching beats, serrated guitars, and clipped vocals, with each syllable inspected, stamped, and sent down the conveyor belt. Sparks supplies the arch pop theatre, while DEVO’s mechanized discipline tightens the arrangement into nervous obedience. Sigue Sigue Sputnik adds tabloid chrome and cheap-thrill futurism; Adam and the Ants lend the proceedings enough rouge, regalia, and heroic excess to turn emotional collapse into prime-time entertainment. Through it all, the robotic chant of “we are sex machines” passes from come-on to diagnosis. Lamandé opens the video in daylight, where a striped-sleeved interviewer, Ruben Pol, carries a star-marked microphone through a narrow service alley. An elderly woman in a floral dress, a woman in pink, a muscled, semi-shirtless man wearing an enormous silver “S,” and several other passersby take their turns before the camera. They offer no opinions or explanations; instead, each stranger lip-syncs Pol’s account of physical appetite and emotional vacancy. Stark title cards and white-background close-ups give the sequence the air of a public-information broadcast commandeered by style and libido. The assignment soon strays underground. The cast descends into a concrete parking garage, crowds the reporter, gathers around a car, and carries a cardboard placard commanding viewers to REPENT. Pol eventually perform before a packed room and a hard white backlight as the same faces press toward the handheld camera. What began as an orderly street interview becomes a collective compulsion, collapsing the distance between observer, participant, stranger, and former lover. A final outtake catches the brothers laughing together, briefly breaking the program’s immaculate pose. “It started off with the idea of doing an interview style video with a diverse cast of characters,” the band explain. “We liked the idea of ‘strangers’ singing the song, similarly how the two ex-lovers in the lyrics are acting like strangers. We shared the idea with director Remi Lamandé who brought the full script to life.” Watch the video for Sex Machines below: “Sex Machines” is available through Bandcamp and other streaming platforms. Listen below, and order here. Sex Machines by Pol Pol introduced their analogue-driven edge with a self-titled debut EP in 2023. The subsequent singles “Masks” and “The Chameleon” moved deeper into theatrical New Romantic territory, establishing the brothers as musicians whose presentation carries as much intent as the recordings themselves. The duo oversees their visuals, videos, merchandise, and fanzines themselves. Their first zine, documenting a Western European tour, is stocked by the Paris bookshop Librairie 1909. That multidisciplinary practice has also led to sound-design collaborations with Louis Vuitton, Miu Miu, and others. In early 2026, Pol opened sold-out Lebanon Hanover shows in London, Lille, and Paris. With “Sex Machines,” their private machinery has moved into public view, microphone extended and camera rolling, only to discover that the whole crowd already knows the refrain. items.body: Twenty-five years is enough time for a cult film to acquire the patina of a period piece, but Gypsy 83 has always been preoccupied with people who regard the present tense as something to survive. Todd Stephens’s 2001 road trip movie follows two goth outsiders in Sandusky, Ohio: Gypsy Vale, played by Sara Rue, and her younger friend Clive Webb, played by Birkett Turton, whose devotion to Stevie Nicks offers both an aesthetic vocabulary and a plausible escape route. When they hear about New York City’s Night of 1000 Stevies, they climb into a car and head east, hoping that Gypsy might finally step onto a stage large enough for the person she imagines becoming. This month, the film is heading back to theaters in a considerably updated form. Gypsy 83: The Director’s Cut has been restored in 4K from the original 35mm camera negative and expanded to 138 minutes, compared with the 95-minute version released in 2001. More than forty minutes of previously unseen material have been restored, along with nine additional music tracks. The new edition opened at New York’s Quad Cinema on August 14 and begins a Los Angeles engagement at the Nuart Theatre on August 21, with additional screenings scheduled around the United States through September. For a movie so steeped in black clothes, pale faces, record collections, and the private language of fandom, Gypsy 83 has a surprisingly capacious heart. Gypsy and Clive are bonded by the sense that the lives available to them in Sandusky have already been written by other people. Their trip to Manhattan gives the film its engine, though Stephens is equally interested in the smaller humiliations and revelations that accumulate along the highway, where the pair encounter strangers whose desires prove no simpler than their own. The legendary Karen Black appears as Bambi LeBleau, a faded lounge singer whose theatricality gives the travelers a glimpse of adulthood as both performance and improvisation. John Doe, of X, plays Gypsy’s father, Ray, while Paulo Costanzo and Anson Scoville round out a cast populated by characters who seem to exist just beyond the borders of respectable small-town life. The film places goth culture within an American road-movie tradition usually reserved for cowboys, drifters, runaways, and seekers, allowing eyeliner, Stevie Nicks devotion, queer longing, and friendship to occupy the passenger seat without requiring translation. The film also occupies a central place in Stephens’s career. After writing and producing the 1998 coming-of-age film Edge of Seventeen, he made his directorial debut with Gypsy 83. Those two films, followed two decades later by Swan Song, form the Ohio trilogy through which Stephens has repeatedly returned to Sandusky, his hometown, as a setting for queer lives formed within the constraints of a Midwestern city. Stephens and editor Anderson Matthew recut the picture from scratch, a process that ultimately stretched across several years. Stephens has said that locating the original negative required detective work after the New York laboratory that had stored it went out of business; the material was eventually traced to a vault in California. The recovered 35mm elements became the basis for the new 4K restoration. Music, always central to the film’s conception of identity, has also been given more room. The restored soundtrack draws on The Cure, Cocteau Twins, Echo & the Bunnymen, Switchblade Symphony, Ministry, Alien Sex Fiend, and Clan of Xymox, alongside Diva Destruction’s cover of “Talk to Me” and Nobody’s Wolf Child’s rendition of “Song to the Siren.” The added material changes more than the running time: songs that once functioned as cultural shorthand can now inhabit scenes at greater length, giving the characters more space to live inside the music that helped them invent themselves Altered Innocence is handling the new theatrical release. After its August 14–20 run at Quad Cinema, the film plays Los Angeles from August 21–27, followed by Seattle on August 26 and 27, San Francisco on August 27, Houston on August 29, Nashville on August 31, Philadelphia on September 3, and Denver on September 11. A home-video release is planned for later this year. A quarter-century after Gypsy and Clive first pointed their car toward Manhattan, their destination may be the least interesting part of the trip. What has endured is the film’s understanding of subculture as a form of shelter: the clothes, songs, heroes, jokes, and gestures through which isolated people recognize one another before they have found a more permanent place to belong. The Director’s Cut returns to that idea with forty additional minutes and the advantage of time, allowing Stephens to revisit a film that once left him wounded and finally present the version he had been carrying with him all along. In US cinemas now. Full dates and tickets can be found here. Blu-ray and streaming will follow in November 2026. items.body: Grief has a strange relationship with distance. The dead may be unreachable in any practical sense, yet the mind keeps inventing routes toward them: dreams, remembered voices, photographs, coincidences that briefly acquire the weight of messages. Frankie Rose describes that nocturnal search with the rueful humour of someone who knows how unreliable the equipment can be. Her latest single, Return To Dust, has intense emotional gravity. Drawn from Rose’s forthcoming album Hila, the song treats grief as a condition in which perception grows unstable, opening possibilities that daylight tends to dismiss. Rose’s voice hangs high in the arrangement, cool and clear against drums and synthesizers with considerable physical force beneath them. There are echoes of Enya’s suspended grandeur, PJ Harvey’s severity, the private ache of Cat Power, and the voluptuous gloom of Portishead; elsewhere, the guitar and vocal textures recall Cocteau Twins and the ceremonial grandeur of Siouxsie and the Banshees. Rose has spent much of the past fifteen years refining her ability to make scale and solitude coexist. On Return To Dust, enormous spaces seem to open around a voice that remains remarkably intimate. The production has breadth without sacrificing detail, with each layer contributing to an impression of drifting farther from familiar coordinates while carrying something painfully terrestrial along for the ride. “In my dreams I travel the cosmos and the astral realm looking for ones I’ve lost,” says Frankie Rose. “But I’m a pretty bad receiver, and I am pretty sure I keep missing what they’re trying to tell me.” The self-directed video literalizes Rose’s celestial preoccupations with a playful montage that sends her wandering through the cosmos. She floats among stars and planetary vistas, appearing less like an astronaut conquering unknown territory than a traveller amusing herself while attempting an impossible form of correspondence. The homemade theatricality is crucial. Rather than turning bereavement into solemn science fiction, Rose permits herself whimsy, introducing the peculiar comedy of trying to locate the dead somewhere beyond the visible universe. The video’s cosmic scenery therefore feels less like escape than an extension of mourning itself. Loss can make ordinary reality seem insufficient, sending the imagination searching for some hidden frequency on which absence might become communication. Rose understands the absurdity in that desire and allows it to remain absurd without diminishing its emotional force. Somewhere beyond the planets, perhaps, a message is being transmitted. For now, she is still turning the dial. Watch the video for Return To Dust below: The tension between wonder and uncertainty runs throughout Frankie Rose’s forthcoming album Hila. “Hila is a record about loss,” she says. “What persists beyond the range of ordinary perception? The place mourning keeps returning to — not quite transcendence, not quite doubt. The edge of what we can see.” Self-produced in Rose’s home studio after extensive touring with The Jesus & Mary Chain and Swervedriver, the album also features drummer Justin Welch, known for his work with Elastica and Lush. Its darker passages draw from the esoteric menace of later Coil, the bodily propulsion of Skinny Puppy, and the otherworldly pop vocabulary associated with Cocteau Twins. Yet Return To Dust suggests that Rose’s fascination with these references has become increasingly personal. Genre provides the architecture; bereavement supplies the strange new physics. Listen to Return To Dust below and order the single here. Hila is out September 18 via Born Losers Records worldwide outside the EU and UK, and Night School Records in the EU and UK. Order vinyl here. items.body: Berlin art-pop and indietronica artist Gene Sophia Bogolepov release “Slow Down Your Burning” on 3 September 2026 through MYCELM, the label and archive Bogolepov run from the same city. It is the first single from “Dråma”, a nine-track album set for 11 November 2026, and it carries the darkwave and experimental edges that have run through the project since its move to Germany. The album will be sold through Bandcamp, Qobuz and the MYCELM platform. It will not appear on Spotify in full. MYCELM states that the omission follows the artist’s ideological beliefs, so the album is being kept off the largest streaming service by choice rather than by a licensing gap. “Dråma” was assembled by a small group. Diego Ferri handled guitars, production and engineering, Volodymyr Nestryga played drums and percussion, Dimitri Klochkov contributed guitars, bass and synths, and Scout Hansen co-wrote. Piano parts came from Andrian Lebedev, who died in 2021. How ‘Dråma’ began, four days before the invasion On 20 February 2022, four days before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Bogolepov was in the studio with Scout Hansen, working while anxious about what was coming. “Serpent Song” came out of that session, written from inside the mind of a psychopath, and the rest of the album grew around it over the four years that followed. MYCELM describes the result as “an album about faith, justice, violence, and what happens when catastrophe becomes ordinary.” The 2017 song “Mother Russia” drew enough hostility in Russia to push the artist into exile, and the move to Berlin reset the project. “Art Brut” followed in 2021. Onstage the current line-up is a duo: Bogolepov with Diego Ferri, a Berlin musician and sound engineer who played guitar for and produced the Canadian lo-fi act Michelle Gurevich, and whose other credits take in BBC1 and work with Martin Bisi, the New York producer behind records by Sonic Youth and Swans. Recent appearances include Ms Artville Festival in Hamburg in 2021, Noorderzon Festival in Groningen and WORM in Rotterdam in 2022, Berghain in 2024 and LARK in Berlin in 2025. MYCELM has also submitted the album to Wave-Gotik-Treffen 2027. No 2027 WGT line-up has been announced, so no booking is confirmed. About Gene Sophia Bogolepov Gene Sophia Bogolepov grew up in a working-class household in Saint Petersburg, surrounded by family instruments, and first performed in 2003. The early electropunk project T-Lazarus came out of that period, followed by the electro-rock band Gender ID, which played across Russia and Europe on bills with Ladytron, Placebo, Editors, Sparks and Apparat Band. Two further projects, Dukes of Betelgeuse and Ego Collider, ran alongside them. In 2013 Bogolepov adopted the name 1314 and turned the work towards living with HIV, anxiety and queer isolation. The 2017 anti-authoritarian song “Mother Russia” produced a backlash that led to exile, and Berlin became the base from then on. “Art Brut” arrived in 2021, and the catalogue collected on the MYCELM platform now runs from “Ultrawhite” and “Home Kids & Bathroom Romance” through “[bodies] EP”, “Deviant Comedy”, the 1314 LP, “Art Brut”, “Long Awaited Silence Of Mind (坂本龍一に捧げる)”, the “Titanium” EP and the “Art Brut (Mycelium Edition)” reissue. MYCELM itself began as Mycelium, a paywalled discography archive, and relaunched under its current name in February 2026 as what Bogolepov describes as an archive, community and label for underground and unsigned artists, most of them queer. It publishes as Mycelm Records and Mycelm Publishing out of Berlin, and it now handles both “Slow Down Your Burning” and “Dråma”.

items.body: Nocturnal Culture Night returns to Kulturpark Deutzen from 4 to 6 September 2026, with its traditional Warm-Up taking place on Thursday, 3 September. Now at edition number 19, NCN once again uses several stages to accommodate a programme that reaches well beyond any single definition of goth, industrial or electronic music. The 2026 bill shows that range plainly. Nik Kershaw, Die Krupps, SKYND, Diary of Dreams, Peter Heppner & Band, L’Âme Immortelle, Girls Under Glass, Samsas Traum / Weena Morloch, Siglo XX, Esplendor Geométrico, Pankow, Actors, Sierra Veins, The Beauty Of Gemina, HORSKH, Mildreda, Melotron, Of The Wand & The Moon and Container 90 are the most familiar names on the bill, and they come from very different points in electronic and alternative music history. The festival takes place in Kulturpark Deutzen, roughly 30 kilometres south of Leipzig. NCN stays small by design, with the festival shop describing a capacity of around 2,500 visitors. The programme is spread across the Amphibühne, Waldbühne, Parkbühne and Kulturbühne, alongside the separate Lesebühne. From 300 people to NCN 19 The first Nocturnal Culture Night took place in 2005 with approximately 300 visitors. Holger Troisch had begun developing the idea two years earlier, and that first edition was much smaller than the present festival: one stage and barely a full day of concerts. The growth that followed did not turn NCN into a conventional large festival. Four music stages have been in operation since 2014, while different parts of the programme gradually acquired their own musical emphasis. The Parkbühne, for example, became associated with synth, coldwave, minimal and post-punk from 2016 onwards; the Kulturbühne developed a stronger relationship with neofolk, industrial and experimental work. 2026 is officially NCN 19, while the organisers regard 2027 as the twentieth jubilee edition. The chronology does not correspond directly to twenty consecutive calendar years because there was no regular second edition in 2006 and the pandemic period produced separate special editions. NCN is currently operated through NCN Event GmbH, based in Leipzig, with Holger Troisch remaining the festival’s organiser. Holger Troisch and a festival with no single genre Troisch’s approach to booking explains much of the 2026 programme. Years ago he summarised the balance: “The line-up, the festival lives by big and successful names, but also by insiders.” He followed it with an even simpler statement: “Versatility is important for me.” (Reflections of Darkness, 2017) His more recent comments say the same. Discussing NCN’s identity in 2026, Troisch said that the festival had become too broad musically to tie itself to a single genre, and that introducing new styles was necessary if the event itself was to continue developing. The running order shows that principle more clearly than an alphabetical line-up. On Saturday alone, Nik Kershaw closes the Amphibühne, SKYND headline the Waldbühne, Actors occupy the evening Parkbühne slot, and Esplendor Geométrico close the live programme on the Kulturbühne. Those artists do not belong to one genre or even one generation. They share NCN’s long-standing remit: electronic, post-industrial, dark and alternative music in the broadest sense. Nik Kershaw: an unusual headliner for NCN The most conspicuous name this year is Nik Kershaw, who closes the Amphibühne on Saturday at 22:30. Kershaw’s breakthrough came in 1984, with “Wouldn’t It Be Good”, “I Won’t Let the Sun Go Down on Me” and “The Riddle”. His official biography records 62 weeks on the UK Singles Chart across 1984 and 1985, and he performed at Live Aid in 1985. His later career took in songwriting and production for other artists alongside his own releases and performances. He is not a darkwave or industrial artist, and NCN does not try to redraw his history to make him fit. The festival has long treated the wider electronic and alternative culture of the 1980s as part of its remit rather than limiting itself to artists carrying a particular scene label. Kershaw sits at one end of the festival’s historical spectrum: highly crafted British electronic pop that entered mass culture in the 1980s. Only a few hours earlier, other stages will be presenting EBM, post-punk, industrial electronics and experimental music that developed around or against that same decade. Die Krupps: the industrial line runs directly through Düsseldorf On Sunday the Amphibühne closes with Die Krupps, whose place in this programme needs less explanation. The Düsseldorf group began with the industrial construction of “Stahlwerksinfonie” before “Wahre Arbeit Wahrer Lohn” and subsequent releases developed a hard electronic language closely associated with the foundations of EBM. During the 1990s, metal guitar was folded into that vocabulary, creating the electronic-metal combination that became another major strand of the band’s identity. Die Krupps marked 45 years of activity in 2025. Their current phase is not limited to anniversary performances: the band signed a multi-album agreement with Dependent Records, with a new album announced for 2026, and guitarist Marcel Zürcher returned to the group in June 2026. The band’s own announcement specifically lists NCN among the concerts following his return. There is also a long NCN connection. The festival archive lists Die Krupps in 2015, 2018, 2023 and 2026, making this their fourth appearance in Deutzen. SKYND: industrial music through the architecture of true crime SKYND close Saturday’s Waldbühne at 21:00 and represent a much newer form of industrial performance. The project is built around vocalist SKYND and producer/multi-instrumentalist F, with its catalogue structured around real criminal cases. Rather than using true crime as occasional imagery, the project has made it the organising principle of its music, videos and visual identity. Its own description is simply “TRUE CRIME MUSIC.” The project has released steadily through 2026. Material from “Chapter VII: Red Winter” has included pieces concerning Andrei Chikatilo, Tamara Samsonova and Mikhail Popkov, while the subsequent “Jimmy Savile” opened Chapter VIII: The Open Secret, shifting attention towards institutional protection and the mechanisms that allowed abuse to remain concealed. The NCN set lands in the middle of that run of releases. Diary of Dreams: five appearances across the history of NCN Diary of Dreams play the Waldbühne at 19:25 on Sunday. Adrian Hates’ project has run for more than three decades on electronic production, darkwave structures, guitars and inward songwriting. The current release is “Chapter 1: Dead End Dreams”, while the band continue touring extensively through 2026. Their NCN history is long. The official archive lists appearances in 2007, 2009, 2013, 2021 and 2026, making this their fifth visit. Repeat bookings shape the festival’s history as much as new ones. Some projects come back at intervals long enough for NCN to have documented how their work and their audience changed. Peter Heppner & Band Peter Heppner & Band play the Amphibühne at 17:20 on Sunday, immediately before Die Krupps later that evening. Heppner’s own site confirms the full-band NCN appearance on 6 September 2026. It will be his third NCN, following appearances in 2014 and 2020. Heppner and Die Krupps on the same main stage shows how NCN handles German electronic history. One represents a melodic, vocal-driven lineage closely associated with synthpop and dark pop; the other comes directly from industrial music and EBM. NCN does not collapse those histories into one genre, but it does recognise that their audiences have overlapped for decades. L’Âme Immortelle and Girls Under Glass Friday brings two other established names whose careers have repeatedly crossed the boundaries between electronics, goth and heavier music. L’Âme Immortelle, appearing at 21:25 on the Waldbühne, were founded in Austria in 1996 and are centred on Thomas Rainer and Sonja Kraushofer. The male/female vocal contrast has stayed central to the project while the music itself has moved between dark electronics, rock and more melodic material. The group will mark its 30th anniversary in 2027 with a dedicated concert series. This is their second NCN appearance after 2016. Girls Under Glass, meanwhile, close Friday’s Amphibühne. Their history reaches back to the mid-1980s and encompasses wave, gothic rock, electronics and industrial influences rather than a single fixed style. NCN has hosted them in 2010, 2016, 2022 and now 2026. Siglo XX, Pankow and Esplendor Geométrico: the historically important names are not all on the main stage Some of the historically important bookings are positioned away from the Amphibühne. Belgium’s Siglo XX, appearing at 21:25 on Friday’s Parkbühne, emerged in Genk in 1978 and became an important part of the austere Belgian post-punk and coldwave history of the period. The NCN archive lists 2026 as their first visit to the festival. Pankow, playing Friday on the Waldbühne, represent a different European trajectory. The Florence project developed from the Italian experimental underground into harder electronic and industrial territory and later became strongly associated with EBM. They return to NCN after a previous appearance in 2016. Then there is Esplendor Geométrico, closing Saturday’s Kulturbühne at 22:45. The Spanish project dates to 1980, and its repetitive, physical combination of mechanical rhythm, noise and industrial electronics developed largely outside the Anglo-German narratives through which industrial music is often described. NCN 19 will be their first appearance at the festival. That booking is the kind Troisch’s distinction between “big names” and “insiders” covers: historical weight and billing size are not the same thing. Actors, Sierra Veins, HORSKH and the current generation The contemporary programme Several of the contemporary acts arrive with new material rather than a back catalogue. Canadian ACTORS take the 21:00 Parkbühne slot on Saturday, returning to NCN after their first appearance in 2019. The Vancouver band have released steadily through 2026: “CTRL” appeared in February, followed by the DJ? Acucrack reworking “Dead Inside (Crackmix)” in March, “Left On Read” in April and “Youth” in July. The latter arrives while ACTORS are working on a new album, their first studio record since Acts of Worship and Reanimated. The singles keep the tightly constructed post-punk songwriting the band are known for, but the production hits harder: stronger electronic rhythm, more low-end pressure and a closer relationship with the dancefloor. NCN catches ACTORS mid-change rather than between records. Sierra Veins closes the Parkbühne at 00:10 on Friday, a late slot that suits how far her work now runs past darkwave into techno and harder club music. Her second full-length album, “In The Name Of Blood”, was released on 7 November 2025 and made the change from SIERRA to SIERRA VEINS part of the record’s central subject: identity, inheritance and the traces carried within us. It also includes the collaboration “Memory Cells” with Ghost Dance. In February 2026 she followed it with “HypnoVizion 031: SIERRA VEINS (DJ Mix)”, a 46-minute mix for REZZ’s HypnoVizion series that places her own tracks and remixes beside material from artists including Gesaffelstein, Boys Noize, Matteo Tura and Ghost Dance. The album and the mix place her at NCN with one foot in the dark electronic scene and the other in a much wider club culture. French trio HORSKH open the Parkbühne programme on Friday, three weeks before the release of their new ten-track album “MTNT” on 25 September 2026. Three pieces from this phase have already appeared: “Bad Glitch” in January, “Hyperhuman” in March and “Glow” in June. HORSKH themselves describe the project as neo-industrial / grunge / metal. The new material continues the collision between electronic programming, heavily processed vocals, distorted guitars and industrial rhythm that sets them apart from acts rebuilding an older industrial vocabulary. The NCN set is one of the last festival dates before MTNT is out. Belgium’s Mildreda, appearing on the Waldbühne at 14:20 on Sunday, arrive in Deutzen even closer to a new record. “Realities” is released by Dependent Records on 28 August 2026, just nine days before the NCN performance. The eighteen-track double album follows Blue-Devilled and pushes Jan Dewulf’s dark electro past the colder boundaries usually associated with the genre. The structure expands too: recurring “Reality Check” pieces divide the album, while Johan Van Roy of Suicide Commando appears on “Virtual Goddess” and Constantin “Breñal” Warter of Calva Y Nada guests on “Rückwärts.” The first single, “End of the Line,” appeared in June, followed in July by “Virtual Goddess”; Dewulf has described the latter as a confession rather than a criticism of social media: the contradiction between seeking meaningful connection and still responding to the tiny rewards of digital approval. He also says the writing brought colours and emotions into Mildreda that had sat outside his comfort zone, rather than extending the sound of Blue-Devilled. The NCN set is one of the first chances to hear how that studio material works live, against a show built on Dewulf’s vocals and electronics and Christophe Salvatore’s keyboards. Around them, The Foreign Resort, Mayflower Madame, Winter Severity Index, SIIE, Debdepan, Lovataraxx, Lone Assembly, Grundeis, Container 90, Ambassador 21, Menticide, AD and Intent extend the contemporary programme in very different directions. They are not one new generation of “dark music”. The schedule shows post-punk, EBM, industrial electronics, synth-driven music and club culture overlapping without becoming interchangeable, and the separate stages keep those distinctions visible. The acoustic, ritual and experimental side The Kulturbühne runs its own programme. Of The Wand & The Moon close the stage on Sunday, while Corde Oblique, Cawatana, Darkwood, Paganland, Tears Of Othila, Nemuer, SIAMGDA ꕾ Marie, Supersimmetria and MS Gentur + Sven Phalanx occupy points between neofolk, ritual sound, experimental electronics, ambient and industrial music. Those artists would lose their context between larger electro acts on a main stage. Splitting the site lets NCN stay broad without pretending all of its music is interchangeable. The running order shows Troisch’s booking method in practice. A British pop songwriter with a 1980s chart catalogue goes on one stage, Spanish industrial pioneers on another, true-crime industrial performance on a third and neofolk or experimental electronics elsewhere, with none of them redefined to make the combination work. NCN’s identity rests on which strands still make sense for the same audience in the same weekend, not on holding a genre boundary. After nineteen editions that is still a booking question. About Nocturnal Culture Night Nocturnal Culture Night has been staged at Kulturpark Deutzen in Saxony since 2005, when Holger Troisch opened the first edition on a single stage for roughly 300 visitors. The site sits in the village of Deutzen, part of the municipality of Neukieritzsch, about 30 kilometres south of Leipzig, and its wooded amphitheatre and surrounding buildings gave the festival its four-stage layout from 2014 onwards. Troisch has run the event throughout, latterly through NCN Event GmbH in Leipzig, and the programme covers EBM, industrial, post-punk, coldwave, synthpop, neofolk, ritual and experimental electronics side by side rather than in separate weekends, with a Lesebühne carrying readings by German genre authors in parallel with the music. The 2026 line-up reached its present shape after a change at the top of the bill. Marc Almond was announced as the first NCN 19 headliner in September 2025, then withdrew on health grounds; Nik Kershaw was booked in his place for the Saturday Amphibühne slot. Camping and non-camping weekend tickets and day tickets are sold only through the official NCN shop, and caravan and parking tickets sold out earlier in the year. The 2027 edition is the one the organisers count as the twentieth jubilee, which makes NCN 19 the last edition before that anniversary.

items.body: Dutch new wave duo Pol released the official video for “Sex Machines” on 21 August 2026. Fashion photographer and filmmaker Rémi Lamandé directed it. The single itself came out on 25 June 2026 as a two-track digital release on Bandcamp, pairing the 3:59 vocal version with an instrumental of the same length, and is also on streaming platforms. Pol are the brothers Ruben and Matthijs Pol, who are based in Paris. They gave “Sex Machines” a single launch show during Paris Fashion Week in June 2026, two months before the video appeared. How Pol built the ‘Sex Machines’ video Lamandé built the clip as a street interview programme. Ruben Pol carries a star-marked microphone through a service alley and holds it out to a series of passers-by, each of whom lip-syncs the lyric instead of answering. The cast then moves into a concrete parking garage, and the closing section shows the duo performing to a packed room under hard white backlight. A final outtake shows the two brothers laughing. The duo explained where the concept started: “It started off with the idea of doing an interview style video with a diverse cast of characters. We liked the idea of ‘strangers’ singing the song, similarly how the two ex-lovers in the lyrics are acting like strangers. We shared the idea with director Remi Lamandé who brought the full script to life.” The brothers wrote and produced the track themselves. Matthijs Pol plays drum computer, electric guitar, synths, xylophone and sings; Ruben Pol plays drum computer, electric guitar, synths, bass, vocoder and sings. Matthijs and Ruben mixed it with Paul D. Millar, and Gianni Peri mastered it. On their own Bandcamp page the duo describe the song as built on “twitching beats, serrated guitars and clipped vocals”. Sex Machines by Pol About Pol Pol is a duo formed by the Dutch brothers Ruben and Matthijs Pol, now based in Paris, France. Both play guitar, synthesizers and drum computer and both sing; Ruben adds bass and vocoder, Matthijs adds xylophone. The pair write, produce and mix their own recordings and handle their visuals, videos, merchandise and fanzines themselves. The brothers issued a self-titled debut EP in 2023. Two singles followed on their own Bandcamp: “Masks” in June 2024 and “The Chameleon” in December 2024. Their first zine, which documents a Western European tour, is stocked by the Paris bookshop Librairie 1909, and the same multidisciplinary practice has produced sound-design work for Louis Vuitton and Miu Miu. In 2024 the duo played their first headline show at a sold-out Bitterzoet in Amsterdam with Logan Sky of Visage, and have since performed in Europe, the United States and Japan. In early 2026 they opened sold-out Lebanon Hanover shows in London, Lille and Paris. “Sex Machines”, released on 25 June 2026, is their first new music since “The Chameleon”. The Rémi Lamandé video, out on 21 August 2026, is the first visual the duo have released from it.
